details.description:
MaxiMix is an Irwin Hunter pasture blend put together to do what its name suggests: get the most out of a paddock across the whole season rather than producing a single flush.

It combines complementary proven varieties, chosen so that their strengths cover each other. A mix built this way is more forgiving than a single variety sown alone, because different components come away under different conditions, and a season that suits one part of the blend will usually carry the pasture even where another part struggles.

That principle is what sixty years in the seed business teaches. Formulating a mix is a matter of knowing which varieties actually complement one another in local conditions, not simply combining good ones.

MaxiMix is broadly adapted across soil types and produces strongly for both grazing and fodder conservation, with reliable establishment.

It suits growers who want a dependable, high producing pasture without designing the blend themselves, and it can be grazed or shut up for silage or hay depending on how the season develops.
keyAttributes: Maximises pasture potential across the season
Strong production for grazing and conservation
details.seoDescription: This unique combination of different species of pastures provides an excellent mix for achieving a highly productive as well as highly nutritious feed that extends throughout the season.
details.standLifeNotes: It adapts well to loam and gravelly soils, is commonly used in cover crop and regenerative pasture mixes, and provides added benefits of deep rooting, high seed production, and nitrogen fixation. Regeneration is reduced if cut late for silage or hay.

Well suited to shorter growing seasons and a wide range of Western Australian soil and climate conditions, it also offers high leaf rust tolerance.

details.description:
Silahay is built for growers who want bulk feed for the pit or the bale without paying top dollar for it, and it is an Irwin Hunter formulation refined over many seasons of supplying silage and hay producers across the state.

It pairs two proven Western Australian annual ryegrasses with balansa and Persian clovers, and deliberately runs near equal proportions of diploid and tetraploid ryegrass rather than leaning on tetraploids alone.

That formulation choice is the whole point of the mix. Diploid ryegrass seed is smaller and lighter than tetraploid, and the clovers go in uncoated rather than coated, so a bag holds roughly a quarter more actual seeds than a comparable tetraploid-and-coated-clover blend of the same weight. Sown at the same rate per hectare that puts more plants in the ground, and more plants is more dry matter for the same money. The clover component then lifts the quality of what eventually goes into the pit.

The mix establishes with real early vigour and builds bulk quickly through winter into spring, which is what a silage or hay programme needs. It responds strongly to spring fertiliser, and is cut mid spring for silage or left later for hay.

On clean paddocks it can be dry sown ahead of the break where the grower is comfortable with that risk.

Around 25% more seeds per bag than coated mixes

To encourage increased tillering, ensure plants are not prone to pulling, then graze at 6 to 8cm high. Increased sowing rates will increase interplant competition during establishment, offering earlier grazing and higher pasture production where supported with increased fertiliser.

details.description:
The Self Regeneration Pasture Mix was introduced by Irwin Hunter to serve the large number of growers who need an early flowering pasture that will come back on its own, and it is built around certified Safeguard ARGT resistant annual ryegrass.

That choice is deliberate and specific. Annual ryegrass toxicity is a serious problem in Western Australian pasture, and Safeguard is the only annual ryegrass Irwin Hunter will recommend for pasture regeneration in this state, because it flowers early, while there is still time for effective cross-pollination with the resident Wimmera ecotype. That cross-pollination is the mechanism by which resistance is carried into the following year's population, so the paddock becomes progressively safer rather than needing to be resown.

The mix combines that ryegrass with clovers that set seed for regeneration in following years, so the pasture rebuilds itself from a soil seed bank.

It gives growers two things at once: protection against ARGT, and a pasture that regenerates without the cost of resowing. It also provides grazing through winter and early spring before the paddock is locked up for seed set.

details.tagline: Deep rooted and hard seeded
details.description:
Marguerita is a hard seeded French serradella, and it addresses the main limitation of the soft seeded types: their inability to regenerate after a cropping phase.

Its increased hard seededness gives increased persistence, and that persistence has a compounding effect. A stand that comes back reliably over an extended pasture phase produces more total dry matter than one that has to be re-established, and it generates more nitrogen for the crop rotation that follows, so the benefit shows up in both the livestock and the cropping enterprise.

Its growth habit is upright compared with Cadiz, which gives it the potential to be more tolerant of grazing and makes it easier to harvest for seed.

It is moderately tolerant of red legged earth mite, blue green aphid and cowpea aphid, the three pests most likely to damage an establishing serradella, though it is susceptible to lucerne flea and should be monitored where that is present.

Flowering is early, at approximately 114 days at Perth, with a range from 103 to 125 days depending on district.

details.tagline: Very persistent and prolific seeder
details.description:
Dalkeith is an early flowering subterranean clover suited to the shorter growing seasons of the drier wheatbelt, and it has been one of the most widely sown sub clovers in Western Australia for decades.

Early flowering is what fits it to that country. In a district where the season closes in early October, a mid or late maturing clover will not complete seed set, and the stand fails the following year. Dalkeith flowers early enough to finish, which is why it persists where later varieties do not.

It is very persistent and a prolific seeder, building a substantial seed bank in the soil, and its high hard seed levels mean that seed bank is released across several seasons rather than all at once. That is the mechanism behind its reliability through cropping rotations.

Dalkeith suits moderately acidic, well drained soils. It can be used in crop rotations, though it performs best where the pasture phase runs at least two years, giving it time to rebuild seed reserves before the paddock returns to crop.

details.tagline: Year-on-year top performer from Esperance to Perth
details.description:
Abundant is a mid to late season tetraploid annual ryegrass and one of the longest-standing varieties in the Irwin Hunter range. It is a true westerwoldicum type, and since its release in Western Australia it has proved adaptable across a remarkably wide spread of growing conditions, which is the reason it has stayed in the book while other varieties have come and gone.

The plant is upright with broad, dark green leaves and good tolerance of short periods of waterlogging. Where it separates itself is at both ends of the season. Early vigour is excellent, giving genuine early production, and where the crop is managed well with moisture and nutrition behind it, Abundant will push vegetative growth on into late spring rather than shutting down. It was the highest yielding commercial tetraploid in the 2009 Waroona trials and has performed consistently from Esperance through to Perth since.

Being finer stemmed than many tetraploids, it makes excellent silage and hay, and its high forage quality means the conserved feed is worth having rather than simply bulk. It regrows strongly after a cut, often giving an additional grazing on top of the conserved crop.

Abundant suits any farming system chasing increased production over a longer growing season, and it is used by leading dairy farmers across Western Australia. It also forms the ryegrass backbone of several Irwin Hunter mixes.

details.tagline: Fast establishing diploid with high spring yields
details.description:
Achieve is a diploid Italian ryegrass developed to fix two things at once: winter production and speed of establishment. Italian ryegrasses earn their keep in the cool months, and a variety that is slow out of the ground gives away the very production it was sown for.

It carries later season maturity, which pushes high yields into spring, and good tillering that lets it recover well after grazing. Rust resistance is excellent, which matters in a species that can lose quality quickly to leaf disease in a humid spring, and the upright growth habit means the crop stands rather than lodging when it is shut up for hay or silage.

Achieve suits growers with irrigation, districts that catch summer rainfall events, or country where late spring rain can be relied on. It can be oversown into older pastures in autumn to lift winter and spring production, with the benefit carrying into the following summer, or sown as a new pasture alongside appropriate clovers. It also works as a transition crop following summer forage, in place of a perennial grass, where paddocks need remedial work before a full irrigation pasture goes in.

Managed appropriately it will produce high quality grazing and silage for up to two years, and it suits all livestock types.

details.tagline: Late heading, big producer into winter and spring
details.description:
Amass is a tetraploid Italian ryegrass bred for fast seedling establishment and higher winter yields, at the point in the year when feed is most needed and hardest to come by.

Its later heading date is what holds the package together. Because it is slow to run to head, Amass keeps quality well past the point where earlier flowering ryegrasses have gone to stem. In its second year, Italian ryegrasses of this type flower late enough to match vegetative growth to soil moisture that is still there, sometimes into early December. Flowering is what costs a grass its digestibility, since the plant lays down fibre to hold up a seed head, so late flowering and retained quality are the same trait seen from two sides.

The plant tolerates temporary waterlogging and shows good heat tolerance through the warmer months. Under favourable conditions it will carry into a second year rather than finishing as a one-season crop.

Amass is a low cost way to lift production in an existing dairy pasture, undersown to add winter and spring bulk. It suits irrigated country, districts that get summer rainfall events, or areas that can expect late spring rain, and it produces high quality grazing and silage as well as hay.

details.description:
Amazon T is a tetraploid annual ryegrass selected around a single practical problem: the autumn break in Western Australia is not reliable, and a ryegrass that will not come out of the ground on a marginal break has already cost the grower a season.

Fast emergence is therefore the headline trait, backed by large seed and strong establishment. From there it is a high volume dry matter producer, with outstanding winter growth and a large leaf that carries quality into grazing or a hay cut. Rust resistance is exceptional, which is what protects that quality through a humid spring when leaf disease would otherwise take the edge off the crop.

The finer leaf of Amazon T, unusual in a tetraploid, is the reason it eats better than its bulk would suggest. Tetraploids carry more water in the cell and are generally more palatable than diploids, and a finer leaf on top of that gives high quality grazing without giving up yield.

Amazon T is Australian bred, trialled and grown, and suits growers wanting a high yielding annual that will still perform when the season opens late or unevenly. It works as a straight grazing option, as a hay crop, or as a productive component in an annual ryegrass mix.

details.tagline: Very low endophyte ryegrass that helps stop staggers
details.description:
Ausvic is a perennial ryegrass bred to solve an animal health problem rather than an agronomic one. Most perennial ryegrasses carry an endophyte, a fungus living inside the plant that protects it from insect attack but also produces alkaloids that cause ryegrass staggers in grazing stock. Ausvic was selected to carry very low endophyte, and it was designed to stop staggers.

That decision costs the plant some insect protection, so the rest of the variety had to make up for it. Ausvic is Australian bred from Australian plants and was selected for improved persistence, which is where a low endophyte ryegrass is usually most vulnerable. It is produced under Plant Breeders Rights and is quality assured, so what goes in the bag is what was bred.

It suits producers running stock classes where staggers is a genuine risk and the cost of it, in lost condition and in management time, outweighs the insect tolerance that a high endophyte line would bring. It works under both set stocking and rotational grazing.

Where insect pressure is severe, Ausvic is better used as part of a mixed sward than as a sole grass.

products.descriptionSource: Rewritten from master catalogue tech sheets

details.blurb: A diploid annual ryegrass that establishes fast and recovers quickly after grazing. details.tagline: Fast to establish with quick recovery after grazing
details.description:
Diploid Tetila is a reworking of a well known variety. The original Tetraploid Tetila began as a diploid before it was chemically treated to double its chromosome number, and this variety returns to that diploid form deliberately, to recover advantages the tetraploid conversion had given away.

The differences show up in three places. The leaf is finer, which lifts feed quality and makes the crop better suited to hay and silage after grazing, because fine leaves and stems hold their quality longer in the windrow. Recovery under hard grazing is quicker than the old Tetila managed. And because diploid seed is smaller than tetraploid seed, a bag holds more individual seeds, so the same plant population can be established from about thirty per cent less seed by weight.

That last point is a straightforward cost saving per hectare, and it is the reason the variety is often described simply as the cost effective option.

Diploid Tetila establishes well with good winter production and is highly palatable, with high animal intake. It is produced under an accredited seed care production scheme, so varietal purity is maintained through the supply chain.

Its mid maturity is what suits it to that country. Mid maturity sits between the two, and lets Dunstan finish strongly in a season that turns out better than expected.

It produces high quality feed through winter and spring, is densely tillered, and carries strong rust resistance, which is the trait that protects quality in the second half of the season when leaf disease usually arrives.

Dunstan is best used as the perennial backbone of a pasture plan rather than a short-term fix, sown with clovers and, where appropriate, herbs, to build a sward that carries stock across several years rather than one.

details.tagline: Mid-late maturity with high dry matter and rust resistance
details.description:
Hypa is a mid to late maturing annual ryegrass built around the period between late winter and mid spring, when a pasture is asked to produce the bulk of its dry matter and when quality most often slips away.

Its maturity is what protects that window. By heading later than early maturing annuals, Hypa stays vegetative through the part of the season when feed demand is highest, so growers get bulk and quality together rather than choosing between them.

Rust resistance is high, which is the practical defence of that quality, since leaf rust in a warm humid spring will strip palatability from a susceptible variety just as the crop is at its heaviest. Drought tolerance is good for the type, which gives the crop a better chance of finishing in a season that dries off early.

Hypa suits grazing, silage and hay, and fits growers wanting maximum production concentrated into the late winter to mid spring period rather than spread thinly across a longer season.

details.tagline: Rapid establishment with high winter and spring feed
details.description:
Jackpot is a diploid Italian ryegrass bred with two objectives: rapid establishment with high feed production through winter and spring, and improved persistence, so the stand can produce for two or more years rather than being resown annually.

Those two aims pull in different directions, which is what makes the variety interesting. A grass bred purely for early bulk tends not to last; one bred for persistence is often slow to get going. Testing has confirmed Jackpot performs at least as well as the best cultivars available for both production and survival.

Its heading date is twenty-two days late, and that lateness is where the extended production in spring comes from. High tiller and leaf density keeps the sward dense and productive rather than open and stemmy.

In climates with cool, moist summers, or where growth continues at the end of spring in hotter districts, Jackpot will carry through into a second year. It suits growers wanting more than one season from an Italian ryegrass sowing, and it produces high quality grazing and silage.

details.blurb: A diploid Italian ryegrass selected for rapid establishment and high autumn and winter yields. details.tagline: Fast establishing diploid with strong winter yields
details.description:
Knight is a diploid Italian ryegrass bred for the part of the season that matters most in a pasture system: winter. Winter feed is the most valuable feed a farm can grow and the hardest to buy in, so the brief was a ryegrass that gets away fast in autumn and keeps producing when other grasses slow down.

It is a fast starter, and that early growth is what pays. More growth in autumn means more winter grazings, which in turn sets up a better start to spring, and across several years of Australian trials Knight has produced more dry matter than most other short rotation ryegrasses. The other half of the story is its late heading. Knight flowers around nineteen days later than Nui and throws far fewer aftermath seed heads than other commercially available diploid Italians, so the sward holds quality into late spring and summer instead of running to stem. That combination makes it as useful in the pit or the bale as it is under stock.

Knight suits farms wanting quick winter feed, oversowing into pastures that have thinned out, or a one year grass to extend the growing season. It goes into mixes readily alongside clovers and herbs, and in the right environment it will hold on as a productive two year stand.

Sow it early. Most of Knight's advantage comes from what it does before winter, and a late sowing gives that away.

Mona is a tetraploid Italian ryegrass bred as a replacement for Jeanne, with the aim of combining rapid establishment and high winter and spring feed production with enough persistence to produce for two or more years.

Its defining feature is how late it flowers. At twenty-eight days late it is very late even for an Italian ryegrass, and that extends the period when growers can graze or cut genuinely leafy, high quality forage by up to a month. Crucially, the lateness does not cost the early part of the season: winter and early spring growth are not compromised, which is the usual trade-off with late heading varieties.

It carries a thirty-four per cent yield advantage over the variety it replaces, and produces very little aftermath heading, so quality holds through late spring and into early summer. That matters most for second and third cuts, where a variety throwing seed heads between cuts drops the quality of everything that follows.

Mona is a low cost way to lift production in an existing dairy pasture through undersowing, and it suits irrigated country or districts that receive summer rainfall or late spring rain. The lateness also allows larger, bulkier silage and hay cuts to build farm feed reserves.

New Tetila is a tetraploid annual ryegrass and a long-standing benchmark in the Western Australian market, sold on the basis that it is the quality tetraploid rather than the newest one.

Establishment is excellent with good winter production behind it, and as a tetraploid it is highly palatable, which shows up directly in animal intake. Tetraploid plants carry a higher proportion of cell contents to cell wall than diploids, so stock eat more of what is offered and waste less, and that difference is worth more than a yield figure alone suggests.

It is produced under an accredited seed care production scheme, so varietal purity is maintained through the supply chain and the seed sown is genuinely the variety named on the bag.

New Tetila suits grazing, silage and hay, and remains a cost effective option for growers wanting proven performance rather than a new release. It is also one of the parents of Burst, which sits at a mid-season maturity between New Tetila and Abundant.

Roper also reseeds readily across a range of conditions. That opens up a use most perennials cannot manage. In dryland country where other varieties will not survive as a perennial, roughly north of a line through Donnybrook, Roper can be managed as an annual instead, giving a reseeding pasture that may persist over a number of years if conditions allow.

details.tagline: ARGT resistant ryegrass that cuts poisoning risk
details.description:
Safeguard was developed through a joint programme between the Meat Research Corporation and the South Australian Research and Development Institute to address annual ryegrass toxicity, and it represents a genuine break in a problem that had no good answer before it.

ARGT is caused by a bacterium carried into the seed head by a nematode, and Wimmera ryegrass is the usual host. Safeguard carries resistance to that nematode, and because it crosses with the background Wimmera population, the resistance is passed into the following year's progeny. The paddock therefore gets progressively safer rather than needing to be resown each season. It also lowers ARGT levels in oaten export hay, which protects a market as well as a flock.

Beyond toxicity, Safeguard resists cereal cyst nematode and shows tolerance to the wheat and oat strains of take-all, so it earns its place as a crop disease break in its own right. It flowers at a similar time to Wimmera, which is what allows the cross-pollination to happen, and it produces well through winter and spring for grazing, silage or later hay.

It suits drier cropping and livestock country affected by ARGT, where it is the only annual ryegrass Irwin Hunter will recommend for pasture regeneration.

details.blurb: Highly productive hard seeded species with deep root structure enabling excellent late spring/early summer growth. Adapted to deep acid sands but does not tolerate waterlogging or saline soils. White flower developing pink tinge. Suitable for grazing, hay and silage. Non bloating.

details.tagline: Deep rooted, late flowering aerial clover
details.description:
Arrowleaf is a late maturing annual clover, and its lateness is the whole reason to sow it. Most annual legumes in a Mediterranean system have finished and dried off by the time spring is over, leaving a feed gap before summer forage is available. Arrowleaf keeps producing into that gap, extending the grazing period into summer.

It is deep rooting, which is what allows it to do that. A deep root exploits subsoil moisture that shallower rooted annual legumes cannot reach, so the plant is still growing when others have run out of water. That same root architecture makes it useful for opening up the soil profile.

Dry matter yield is high, and the standing crop suppresses summer weed species that would otherwise take the paddock once the winter pasture has gone. It is an aerial seeding clover with a high proportion of hard seed, which is the basis of its ability to come back year after year.

Arrowleaf also produces seed simply and economically compared to many legumes, which keeps the cost of the pasture phase down and makes it practical to hold a stand over several seasons rather than resowing.

details.blurb: Semi erect cultivar suited to mildly acid-alkaline sandy loam soils with pH 5-8. Tolerant of heavy grazing. Hard seeded with protection against false breaks. Does not produce well in saline or waterlogged soils.
details.tagline: Adaptable across soil types with high hard seed levels
details.description:
Bartolo is a bladder clover, a species chosen for country where the classic sub clovers struggle. It is semi-erect, adaptable across a wide range of soil types, and suited to mildly acid through to alkaline ground, which covers a great deal of the mixed farming zone.

Its defining characteristic is hard seed. Bartolo produces a high level of it, and hard seed is what protects a self-regenerating pasture from a false break. When early rain germinates a paddock and is then followed by a dry spell, soft seeded species lose that year's seedlings entirely; a hard seeded species holds a reserve in the soil that germinates later, and the stand survives.

It tolerates heavy grazing, which matters in a legume expected to persist in a grazed rotation rather than a locked-up seed paddock.

Bartolo does not perform well in saline or waterlogged country, so it belongs on free-draining soils. Where those conditions are met, it is a dependable and widely adapted legume for pasture and cropping rotations.

Berseem is an annual clover grown for one thing above all: bulk of high quality feed in a short time. It is fast growing, highly palatable, and productive enough to be cut several times through a season rather than grazed once and finished.

That multiple-cut ability is what separates it from most annual clovers. Regrowth after cutting is strong, so a stand can be taken for silage or hay and then come again, which suits a grower who wants conserved feed and grazing from the same paddock in the same year.

Nutritionally it is a high quality forage, with the protein and digestibility expected of a well grown clover, and it is highly palatable to all classes of livestock. That combination of quality and sheer bulk is why it is often used in irrigated or high fertility situations where the water and nutrition are available to push it.

Berseem is an annual and does not persist, so it is sown for the season it is needed rather than as a long-term pasture legume, either alone or as the legume component in a short-term ryegrass mix.

Border is a balansa clover selected from long term regenerating stands in South Australia, in fields that had been used for hay, forage and grazed pasture over many years. Plants that had persisted through that management were selected, crossed, and selected again over three cycles.

That selection history explains the traits. It suits growers wanting a legume that will hold on through a wet winter and still produce bulk in spring, either for grazing or for a hay or silage cut.

details.tagline: Suitable for low rainfall areas
details.description:
Casbah is a biserrula, and biserrula occupies a niche few other pasture legumes can fill: genuinely low rainfall country where sub clovers and medics run out of season before they run out of moisture.

Its advantage is a long growing season combined with deep roots. Biserrula continues growing later into spring than most annual legumes, and its root system reaches moisture beyond the range of shallower rooted species, so it produces feed in a period when the rest of the pasture has finished.

It is hard seeded, which gives strong regeneration from the soil seed bank and real resilience against false breaks, and it tolerates acid soils that limit the choice of legume elsewhere.

Casbah suits cropping rotations in the drier districts, where a legume phase has to fix nitrogen and produce feed without demanding rainfall the country does not get. It is best managed to set seed in the establishment year so the seed bank is built before the paddock returns to crop.

details.grazingManagementNotes: Lightly graze in first year to maximise seed set; sown in autumn; twin sowing possible for pure sward

products.name: Coolamon Subterranean Clover
products.descriptionSource: Rewritten from master catalogue tech sheets

details.blurb: Bred by the Department of Agriculture, Western Australia as a replacement for Junee, with slightly later flowering at 125 days at Darkan. Coolamon suits areas above 500mm annual rainfall on well drained, moderately acid soils where the growing season extends into November. It is moderately hard seeded and can be grown in rotation with crops.
details.notes: ⚠ The IH tech sheet attributes Coolamon's breeding to WA Dept of Agriculture, while the NSW DPI Agnote attributes it to NAPLIP (a national program) with development/testing centred in NSW (Wagga Wagga). Both may be technically compatible (WA involved in seed increase, NSW in breeding/selection) but Douglas should verify the correct breeding credit before publishing.
details.tagline: Mid-season replacement for Junee in higher rainfall
details.description:
Coolamon was bred by the Department of Agriculture, Western Australia as a replacement for Junee, and it flowers only marginally later, at 125 days at Darkan against Junee's 124. That near-identical maturity was deliberate: it lets growers substitute one for the other without changing the way the paddock is managed.

What they gain is disease resistance. Coolamon is resistant to clover scorch races 1 and 2, and race 2 is widespread across the Esperance sand plain, where it had been steadily undermining older cultivars. It is also less susceptible to powdery mildew than Junee, though not immune.

It carries only trace levels of formononetin. That matters for anyone joining ewes on clover-dominant pasture, since the oestrogenic isoflavones in some older sub clovers can affect fertility, and a trace-level variety removes the concern.

Coolamon is moderately hard seeded, so it regenerates through a cropping rotation provided the cropping phase is not too long. Increased production means more return per hectare and higher nitrogen inputs for the crop that follows.
details.bredByOrigin: ⚠ Conflicting attribution across sources: IH 2021 tech sheet states Coolamon 'has been bred as a replacement for Junee subterranean clover by the Department of Agriculture, Western Australia'; the NSW
keyAttributes: Resistant to clover scorch races 1 and 2
Higher production lifts return per hectare
Strong nitrogen input for the following crop
Bred as a replacement for Junee
details.standLifeNotes: Coolamon Subterranean Clover is moderately hard seeded and can be grown in rotation with crops, provided cropping frequency is no more than 1 year in 3. Improved persistence compared to other cultivars of similar. When averaged, Coolamon Subterranean Clover has 11% better regeneration density and produces 12% more herbage in autumn / winter, 14% more herbage in spring and 6% more seed production than Junee.
details.diseasePestResistance: Resistant to clover scorch races 1 & 2 (race 2 widespread on Esperance sand plain); resistant to Cercospora leaf spot; susceptible to powdery mildew (less so than Junee); moderately susceptible to leaf rust; some susceptibility to root rots. Coolamon Subterranean Clover is susceptible to powdery mildew, but less so than Junee, and is not likely to cause production losses in grazed situations. Some losses may be possible under favourable conditions for the disease when stands are closed up for hay or seed production.

products.name: Crimson Clover
products.descriptionSource: Rewritten from live website page text

details.blurb: Soft seeded erect annual clover suited to medium-high rainfall areas. Produces a large amount of high quality forage in the late spring period and is adaptable to loam and gravelly soils. Susceptible to germination after false breaks. Often used in mixes for cover crops and regenerative pastures, being deep rooted and having high seed production.
details.notes: [2026 guide] 2026 guide sowing rate is 3 to 10 kg/ha; this row records 'Monoculture: 10 kgs/ha; Mixes: 2 to 5 kgs/ha' — reconcile.
details.tagline: Attractive crimson flowers and highly palatable
details.description:
Crimson clover is an erect annual clover grown for high quality feed through late winter and early spring, and it is one of the most recognisable legumes in a paddock thanks to its deep crimson flower heads.

It is soft seeded, which shapes how it is used. A soft seeded clover germinates readily and establishes fast, but it will not hold a reserve in the soil for future years, so crimson clover is sown for the season rather than relied upon to regenerate. In practice it is used where a grower wants guaranteed establishment and bulk in a single season.

Production is excellent through spring and into early summer, and the plant is highly palatable, so intake is strong. Its erect habit makes it easy to cut, and it is well suited to silage or hay as well as grazing.

It works well as the legume component in short-term pasture and forage mixes, where its speed complements a ryegrass, and it is also valued in cover crop blends for the flowers, which draw pollinators and beneficial insects.
keyAttributes: Highly palatable soft seeded erect annual clover
Excellent spring and early summer production
Suits late winter to early spring grazing
Fast establishing annual for winter feed
details.seoDescription: The clover to make your hay - a deep rooted long season soft seeded aerial seeding clover that is adaptable to a wide range of soil types and management systems in the 500mm and above rainfall zones.
details.grazingManagementNotes: Crimson clover is a highly palatable feed suited to late winter early spring grazing and silage or hay production. To optimise production Crimson clover is best suited to rotational grazing systems allowing recovery time between grazings.

products.name: Diamanti Bladder Clover
products.descriptionSource: Rewritten from master catalogue tech sheets

details.blurb: Diamanti is a highly productive and nutritious winter legume with greater levels of hard seed than Bartolo providing more resilience to false breaks. It flowers earlier and thus can extend further into the drier regions of the Eastern Wheatbelt.
details.notes: ⚠ DOUGLAS SHOULD CHECK: none of these 4 files carry IH Seeds/Irwin Hunter branding, contact details, or disclaimer — they read as LegumeN Pty Ltd / Murdoch University promotional and trial material for a bladder clover cultivar called 'Diamanti' (real name obscured by OCR/trademark-symbol corruption as 'Diaman2ti'). Unclear whether IH Seeds actually distributes this cultivar or simply collected the flyer as market research on a Bartolo competitor/successor. Recommend confirming distribution rights/relationship before publishing this as an IH Seeds product. [2026 guide] The 2026 guide lists this as an IH Seeds product line, which supports resolving the open question on this row about whether IH Seeds distributes the cultivar. Guide print also renders the name as 'Diaman2ti'. Sowing rate was blank on this row and has been filled from the 2026 guide (5 to 10 kg/ha). 2026 guide rainfall is 300mm+; this row records '250 - 400mm' — reconcile.
details.tagline: Productive and nutritious with harder seed than Bartolo
details.description:
Diamanti is a bladder clover developed as an improvement on Bartolo, and the comparison with Bartolo is the clearest way to understand it.

It flowers ten to fourteen days earlier, which suits it to shorter seasons or to fitting a legume phase into a tighter rotation. Its seed is harder, making it more resilient to false breaks, where an early germinating rain followed by dry weather would otherwise wipe out a year's seedlings. Its growth habit is upright rather than prostrate, which makes it considerably easier to harvest, an important practical difference for anyone producing their own seed. And across herbage and seed production it out-yields Bartolo by an average of thirty-five per cent.

It is described as a hay-type bladder clover, offering better nutrition to stock than its predecessor, and it is easily told apart in the paddock by its diamond shaped leaf marker, where Bartolo carries a crescent.

Diamanti suits mixed farming rotations on soils from mildly acid to alkaline, where a productive, reliably regenerating annual legume is wanted between crops.
details.bredByOrigin: Dr B. Nutt and R. Harrison, Murdoch University
keyAttributes: Flowers 10 to 14 days earlier than Bartolo
Harder seed is more resilient to false breaks
Hay-type clover with better animal nutrition
Diamond leaf marker distinguishes it from Bartolo

products.name: Gosse Sub Clover
products.descriptionSource: Rewritten from master catalogue tech sheets

details.blurb: A large white seeded sub clover developed as a replacement for Trikkala, with a prostrate to semi-erect growth habit. Gosse is well suited to moderate to heavy soils and tolerates short periods of waterlogging. As a mid-season maturing clover it suits medium to high rainfall zones with a seven month growth period, and offers improved seedling vigour, increased hard seed at 25%, and better disease resistance.
details.notes: ⚠ 'IH Seeds - Clovers - Gosse sub Clover - Undated v2.docx' is a contaminated/merged file — after the Gosse content it also contains a generic Biserrula paragraph and a complete, differently-worded Trikkala Sub Clover data sheet. Those extra sections were extracted and used as supplementary blurbs for the Casbah Biserrula and Trikkala Sub Clover products respectively; nothing from them was used here.
details.tagline: Large white seeded clover that handles waterlogging
details.description:
Gosse is a large white seeded subterranean clover of the yanninicum group, developed as a replacement for Trikkala. The yanninicum sub clovers are the waterlogging tolerant branch of the species, and Gosse was bred to do that job better.

It tolerates short periods of waterlogging and suits moderate to heavy soils, with a prostrate to semi-erect growth habit. As a mid-season maturing clover it fits medium to high rainfall zones with roughly a seven month growth period.

The improvements over Trikkala are specific: better seedling vigour, higher hard seed at around twenty-five per cent, better disease resistance, and stronger winter and spring herbage production. The hard seed figure is the most consequential, since Trikkala is notably soft seeded and struggles to regenerate through a cropping phase. Greater hard seed levels give Gosse a real seed bank and therefore a future in a rotation rather than only in permanent pasture.

It suits flood-prone flats, heavier soils and irrigated country where waterlogging is a recurring limitation.
keyAttributes: Large white seeded replacement for Trikkala
details.standLifeNotes: With greater hard seed levels, and superior seedling vigour, Gosse is able to establish better plant numbers. Due to a high hard seed level (20-25% v Trikkala 5-10%) Gosse is able to build up a greater reserve of seed in the soil over time, thus enhancing persistence, regeneration and productivity for many years.
details.diseasePestResistance: Resistant to clover scorch; high resistance to phytophthora root rot strains; resistant to pythium root rots, leaf rust and cercospora leafspot; susceptible to red legged earth mite, blue-green aphid, blue oat mite and spotted alfalfa aphid. Gosse was developed for improved seedling vigour, increased hard seed (25%), disease resistance, and winter and spring herbage production. Therefore, control is essential at the early seedling stage and appropriate pest management must be implemented as required.
details.grazingManagementNotes: Do not overgraze too early; light grazing during establishment; heavy grazing to flowering improves seed set; reduce stocking at flowering. Gosse contains very low oestrogen levels and is unlikely to cause any fertility problems to grazing stock. Gosse produces excellent forage for grazing, hay and silage. Light grazing during the establishment period will help control weeds and encourage dense prostrate growth.

products.name: Haifa White Clover
products.descriptionSource: Rewritten from live website page text

details.blurb: Small-medium sized leaves with high winter / early spring activity. Older variety with prolific seed set and some hard seed dispersed by livestock.
details.notes: [2026 guide] 2026 guide sowing rate is 2 to 4 kg/ha; this row records '3 to 4 kgs/ha, plus Ryegrass Clovers. Where sown with other white clovers, adjust the proportion of Haifa accordingly' — reconcile.
details.tagline: Perennial clover for irrigation, a winter producer
details.description:
Haifa is a white clover selected for increased winter activity, with a medium leaf size, and it is used principally as the perennial clover component of irrigated pasture.

Winter activity is the trait that defines it. Many white clovers effectively stop in the cold months, leaving the grass component to carry the pasture through winter without a legume contributing feed or nitrogen. Haifa keeps working, which is why it is described as a winter producer.

It also carries increased stolon density compared to Ladino types. Stolons are the runners by which white clover spreads and repairs itself, and density of stolons is the best single predictor of whether a white clover stand will persist under grazing, so this is a persistence trait rather than a cosmetic one.

The trade-off is at the other end of the year: summer production is limited compared to Ladino types and later releases. Haifa therefore suits systems where winter and spring feed is the priority and summer production comes from elsewhere in the rotation, typically under irrigation alongside a perennial or Italian ryegrass.
keyAttributes: Increased winter activity with medium leaf size
Increased stolon density over Ladino types
details.seoDescription: Haifa white clover is a highly productive winter active variety suited to rotational grazing systems in higher rainfall areas or under irrigation in Western Australia.
details.grazingManagementNotes: Haifa white clover is a highly productive winter active variety suited to rotational grazing systems in higher rainfall areas or under irrigation in Western Australia. With all white clovers it is important to ensure that seed is not sown too deep (maximum 1.5 cm), and that pastures are frequently grazed to ensure light penetration to enhance plant establishment and development.

products.name: Hykon Rose Clover
products.descriptionSource: Rewritten from live website page text

details.blurb: Hard seeded early flowering semi-erect clover with high levels of hard seeds which therefore tolerates false breaks. It has very good insect tolerance. Deep rooted which provides palatable and non bloating forage. Ideal alternative to Serradella in lower pH soils.
details.notes: [2026 guide] 2026 guide sowing rate is 3 to 8 kg/ha; this row records 'Sole Clover with Ryegrass: 6 to 10 kgs/ha; Mixed with other Clovers: 3 to 5 kgs/ha' — reconcile.
details.tagline: Tolerates acid sands
details.description:
Hykon is a rose clover, a species grown for country that defeats most other pasture legumes: acid sands of low fertility, where sub clover will not persist and the alternatives are limited.

Its tolerance of acid sands is the reason to choose it. Rose clovers evolved on poor, light soils and ask relatively little of them, so Hykon will establish and produce where a more demanding legume would fail or need lime and fertiliser it is not worth applying.

It is hard seeded, giving reliable regeneration from the soil seed bank across seasons, and it persists under grazing rather than needing to be locked up.

Hykon suits low fertility sandplain country in mixed farming systems, where the job of the legume is to fix nitrogen and provide some feed on soils that will not carry anything more demanding. It is often sown alongside other hard seeded legumes so that the pasture as a whole covers a wider range of soil types within the paddock.
keyAttributes: Rose clover suited to sandy country
details.seoDescription: Hykon Rose clover is an annual legume with good spring production and is well suited to our Mediterranean-type climate growing satisfactorily on a wide range of soils, but is best suited to areas where sub clover will not grow or grows poorly.
details.grazingManagementNotes: Avoid overgrazing in late spring to protect seed set. Hykon Rose clover is well suited to rotational grazing systems but care needs to be taken when grazed in the late spring period as it is very palatable and if overgrazed seed set can be significantly reduced. It can be sown with other annual legumes and ryegrass and will add good quality to the grazing system especially in the mid to late spring period.

products.name: Izmir Subterranean Clover
products.descriptionSource: Rewritten from master catalogue tech sheets

details.blurb: Seen as the direct replacement for Nungarin in areas receiving less than 375mm annual rainfall. Izmir is early flowering at 78 days but has greater hard seededness than Nungarin, which should give greater persistence in cropping rotations. Seed softening also occurs later in the summer-autumn period, offering more protection from losses due to false breaks.
details.notes: ⚠ Rainfall rate and sow rate figures differ between the 2021 sheet (400mm+; monoculture 10-15kg/ha, mix 6-10kg/ha) and the Undated sheets (350mm+; monoculture 20kg/ha, mix 6-8kg/ha). Used Undated figures as primary since 2 of 3 files agree, but Douglas should confirm which is current.
details.tagline: Early flowering with hard seed for low rainfall
details.description:
Izmir is an early flowering subterranean clover developed as the direct replacement for Nungarin in the lowest rainfall parts of the wheatbelt, and the improvement it offers is in seed behaviour rather than in growth.

It flowers early, at seventy-eight days, which is what allows it to complete seed set in a short season. But where Nungarin is limited by its seed, Izmir carries greater hard seededness, which should give greater persistence through cropping rotations. Just as importantly, its seed softens later in the summer-autumn period, giving it more protection from a false break: when an early rain germinates the paddock and then fails, a variety whose seed has not yet softened still has reserves left in the soil.

Izmir also produces more feed than Nungarin through autumn, winter and spring, and its relatively prostrate growth habit gives good tolerance of grazing. It carries low levels of formononetin.

It is well adapted to moderately acid soils across the northern and eastern zones.
details.bredByOrigin: Referenced from SM008 commercialisation paper: PGH Nichols, GA Sandral, BS Dear, CT de Koning, DL Lloyd, PM Evans, AD Craig, MJ Barbetti, M P You, P Si and PF Smith
keyAttributes: Early flowering with increased winter production
Later seed softening protects against false breaks
Prostrate habit gives good grazing tolerance
details.standLifeNotes: It is early flowering, (78 days), but has greater hard seededness than Nungarin which should result in greater persistence in cropping rotations. The advantage of its higher hard seededness was apparent following seasons where trial sites were either cropped or sprayed out to prevent seed set.
details.diseasePestResistance: Some resistance to clover scorch; low levels of formononetin; greater hard seededness and later seed softening than Nungarin
details.grazingManagementNotes: Relatively prostrate growth habit giving good tolerance to grazing.

products.name: Kyambro Persian Clover
products.descriptionSource: Rewritten from master catalogue tech sheets

details.blurb: Mid season flowering hard seeded Persian. Very persistent if allowed to reseed in first year. Handles wet conditions, has high quality forage and makes higher quality hay than Balansa. Suited to permanent pasture systems. Will tolerate limited salinity.
details.notes: ⚠ Very similar wording (including the identical weaner-sheep growth-rate trial figures: 160g/day vs pasture 50g/day vs Lucerne 90g/day) appears in the separate 'Persian Clover' (generic) and 'Shaftal Persian Clover - 2021 v2' files, suggesting those two files may be re-titled copies of this same underlying generic Persian Clover text rather than distinct cultivar write-ups. See notes on those products.
details.tagline: Thrives in high pH soils
details.description:
Kyambro is a mid season flowering Persian clover, selected as a hard seeded type, and that combination is what makes it useful in permanent pasture rather than only as a one-season forage.

Most Persian clovers are soft seeded and are sown for the year they are needed. Kyambro's hard seed means that if it is allowed to reseed in the first year, the stand becomes very persistent, returning from a soil seed bank season after season.

It thrives in high pH soils, which is unusual and valuable, since alkaline country limits the choice of pasture legume considerably. It also handles wet conditions and tolerates limited salinity, so it suits flats and heavier ground that would defeat a sub clover.

The forage is high quality, and Kyambro makes better hay than balansa clover, which is often the alternative on that sort of country. It suits permanent pasture systems where a durable, high quality legume is wanted on alkaline or seasonally wet soils.
keyAttributes: Mid season flowering and hard seeded
Very persistent if allowed to reseed
details.seoDescription: Kyambro Persian Clover is a self-regenerating annual legume which can produce excellent forage and hay and is suited to the 500mm plus rainfall zones.

products.name: Longhaul Balansa Clover
products.descriptionSource: Rewritten from master catalogue tech sheets

details.blurb: A late flowering, hard seeded balansa with excellent cold tolerance. Its late maturity allows multiple cuts and grazings, with excellent spring production to meet big bulky silage and hay cuts. Longhaul has very good salt tolerance, handles waterlogged soil types, and its deep taproot aids soil conditioning to help moisture move down the profile.
details.notes: Only one source file exists for this product (no 2021 or duplicate versions), and it is a brief bullet-point/table flyer rather than a full tech sheet — considerably thinner than the other Balansa Clover products (Border, Paradana). No botanical background, breeding origin, disease/pest, or full agronomy detail available.
details.tagline: Late flowering, hard seeded and very salt tolerant
details.description:
Longhaul is a late flowering, hard seeded balansa clover, and it was developed as a better option than the balansa varieties that preceded it, Bolta and Viper.

Its late maturity is what growers buy it for. A late flowering balansa keeps growing through the period when earlier types have finished, allowing multiple cuts and grazings from a single stand, and producing the bulk needed for a substantial silage or hay cut in spring.

It carries excellent cold tolerance, which extends the useful growing period at the other end of the season, and very good salt tolerance combined with the waterlogging tolerance the species is known for. That makes it a genuine option on saline, seasonally wet flats where most legumes will not survive.

The deep taproot does work beyond the current season. It opens the soil profile and helps moisture move down rather than sitting at the surface, which improves the ground for what follows.

Being hard seeded, Longhaul regenerates from a soil seed bank, so a stand can be carried across seasons rather than resown.
keyAttributes: Late maturity allows multiple cuts and grazings
Excellent spring bulk for silage and hay
Deep taproot conditions the soil profile
details.standLifeNotes: High hard seed level noted in seed agronomy table. Late flowering hard seeded balansa.
details.grazingManagementNotes: Late maturity allow for multiple cutting and grazing.

products.name: Nungarin Subterranean Clover
products.descriptionSource: Rewritten from master catalogue tech sheets

details.blurb: Early maturing hard black seeded variety with very good persistence due to its high level of hard seeds. More suited to drier areas. Because it is early maturing it does not produce much feed in late spring.
details.notes: No 2021-dated version exists for this product — only a brief 'Summary' tech sheet is available, considerably thinner than most other subterranean clover products (e.g. Dalkeith, Urana) which have full agronomic/disease sections.
details.tagline: Short season variety
details.description:
Nungarin is an early maturing subterranean clover developed for the driest sub clover country, and it is defined by two linked characteristics: a very short season and a very high level of hard seed.

The short season is what lets it survive where the growing period closes early. Nungarin flowers and sets seed before the soil dries, so the stand completes its cycle in years when a later maturing clover would fail entirely.

The high hard seed levels are what make it persistent. Because much of its seed remains hard and ungerminated for several seasons, the soil seed bank is drawn down slowly and the pasture regenerates reliably after a cropping phase.

The cost of that early maturity is late season production. Nungarin does not produce much feed late in the season, because by then it has finished, so growers wanting bulk into spring should look at a later maturing variety and accept the seasonal risk that comes with it.

It is a black seeded variety, and it remains a benchmark for very low rainfall districts.
keyAttributes: Very high hard seed levels for persistence
details.standLifeNotes: Very high level of hard seed yields and good persistence

products.name: Palestine Strawberry Clover
products.descriptionSource: Rewritten from master catalogue tech sheets

details.blurb: A highly adaptable, hard seeded, deep rooted perennial clover with high tolerance of salinity, alkalinity and waterlogging, and of most insect and disease pests that affect other clovers. Palestine is prostrate and slow to establish with poor winter growth, but is generally more persistent than other perennial clovers under grazing. It has high nutritive value and is productive through spring and summer.
details.notes: ⚠ See also the separate, unbranded 'Strawberry Clover' product (Trifolium fragiferum, same species) — its write-up describes an 'upright growth habit' whereas this Palestine-branded sheet describes a 'prostrate' growth habit. Possible inconsistency between the two documents worth checking; treated as two distinct product rows per the source material rather than merged.
details.tagline: Deep rooted perennial for saline and wet ground
details.description:
Palestine is a strawberry clover, a hard seeded, deep rooted perennial legume for country that combines several problems at once: salinity, alkalinity and waterlogging.

Few pasture legumes tolerate all three. Palestine does, which is why it appears on saltland and on seasonally waterlogged flats where the alternatives are limited to a handful of species. It is also tolerant of the majority of insect and disease pests that affect other clovers, so it tends to persist where a more susceptible legume would be gradually eaten out.

The trade-off is at establishment. Palestine is prostrate and slow to establish with poor winter growth, so it does not deliver feed in the first season the way an annual would. What it offers instead is persistence: it is generally more durable under grazing than other perennial clovers, and it is an early maturing type with high levels of hard seed.

Production comes through spring and summer, and nutritive value is high. It suits saline and wet country being managed for the long term rather than a quick pasture fix.
keyAttributes: Deep rooted hard seeded perennial clover
High tolerance of salinity and alkalinity
Tolerant of most clover insects and diseases
More persistent than other perennial clovers
details.standLifeNotes: Generally more persistent than other perennial clovers under grazing, once established. Palestine strawberry clover is a highly adaptable hard seeded, deep rooted perennial clover that performs well in different conditions with high tolerance to salinity, alkalinity and waterlogging. It is an early maturing clover with high levels of hard seededness.
details.diseasePestResistance: Tolerant of the majority of insect and disease pests that affect other clovers
details.grazingManagementNotes: Low seedling vigour — soil should remain damp through germination; tolerates heavy grazing pressure once established. Palestine strawberry clover is prostrate in growth habit and slow to establish with poor winter growth, but generally is more persistent than other perennial clovers under grazing.

products.name: Paradana Balansa Clover
products.descriptionSource: Rewritten from live website page text

details.blurb: Hard seeded annual that exhibits high spring production and excellent water logging tolerance. Will have limited regeneration if cut for late silage or hay. Sets large amount of seeds therefore good for regeneration under appropriate grazing management. Suited to medium to high rainfall areas.
details.tagline: Adaptable, tolerates acid and waterlogged soils
details.description:
Paradana is a balansa clover valued for its adaptability, and it has been a standard choice for difficult country across a wide range of soil types.

Balansa clovers tolerate both acid soils and waterlogging, a combination that rules out many pasture legumes, and Paradana handles both. That makes it useful on flats, on duplex soils that perch water in winter, and on acid country where sub clover struggles.

Production is strong through winter and spring, and the plant produces good bulk, which suits it to silage and hay as well as grazing. It is an aerial seeding annual and regenerates reliably where it is allowed to set seed.

Paradana suits mixed farming systems that need a legume able to hold on through a wet winter and still produce in spring, and it is frequently sown as part of a clover blend so that the pasture covers the range of conditions found within a single paddock.
keyAttributes: Adaptable across a wide range of soils
Good bulk for silage and hay
details.seoDescription: Paradana Balansa Clover is a mid-maturing, semi-erect self-regenerating annual clover selected for its tolerance to waterlogged soils and clover scorch resistant.
details.standLifeNotes: Paradana Balansa Clover can self- regenerate where sufficient moisture is available for seed set.
details.diseasePestResistance: Selected for clover scorch resistance. Paradana Balansa Clover is a mid-maturing, semi-erect self-regenerating annual clover selected for its tolerance to waterlogged soils and clover scorch resistant. It is suited to a wide range of soils in areas where there is a minimum of 450mm annual rainfall and where clover scorch is prevalent.
details.grazingManagementNotes: Lightly graze in 1st year; limit grazing during flowering to allow seed set; graze plant residue in summer to encourage hard seed breakdown; not well suited to rotational grazing (better under continuous grazing). It can grow to over 80cm tall, but ends up prostrate when being grazed. Paradana Balansa Clover helps to increase the legume component of grazed pastures over the late winter and early to mid-spring periods and is particularly useful for early hay production. Plant residue should be grazed during the summer months as this encourages a breaking down of the hard seeds and will maximise re-generation.

products.name: Persian Clover
products.descriptionSource: Rewritten from live website page text

details.blurb: A self-regenerating annual legume that produces excellent forage and hay in the 350mm plus rainfall zones. Regrowth after grazing is excellent and it has high nutritive value as either pasture or hay. The hard seeded Prolific type is an early flowering option selected for early seedling vigour and hard seededness under Western Australian conditions, though being early flowering it is limited in late season production.
details.notes: ⚠ This generic, no-cultivar-name 'Persian Clover' entry is textually almost identical to 'Kyambro Persian Clover' (same weaner-sheep trial figures: 160g/day vs pasture 50g/day vs Lucerne 90g/day) and to the '2021 v2' version of 'Shaftal Persian Clover' (which reuses this exact text under the Shaftal name). It is likely an older/generic species-level listing that predates or parallels the branded Kyambro and Shaftal cultivar sheets, rather than a genuinely distinct product. Recommend Douglas confirm whether this row should be kept separate, merged into Kyambro, or retired given the branded cultivar sheets now exist.
details.tagline: Prostrate clover with high feed value
details.description:
Persian clover is a self-regenerating annual legume that produces excellent forage and hay, and it is one of the more useful legumes on wetter and heavier country.

It is a prostrate clover with high feed value, and regrowth after grazing is excellent, so the same stand can be grazed repeatedly through the season without losing productivity. Nutritive value as pasture or as hay is high.

The hard seeded types are the ones that persist. Prolific, the hard seeded option selected for Western Australian conditions, was chosen for early seedling vigour and for its hard seed, which is what allows the stand to regenerate from a soil seed bank rather than needing resowing. Flowering ranges from around sixty-eight to one hundred and twenty-seven days at Perth, averaging about one hundred and five.

Being an early flowering type, it is limited in late season production, so growers wanting feed deep into spring should pair it with a later maturing legume. It suits the wetter parts of the mixed farming zone and irrigated pasture.
keyAttributes: High nutritive value as pasture or hay
Early flowering with good seedling vigour
details.seoDescription: Persian clover is a tall upright self regenerating annual legume which can produce excellent forage and hay and is suited to the 450mm plus rainfall zones.
details.standLifeNotes: Persian clover is a self regenerating annual legume which can produce excellent forage and hay and is suited to the 350mm plus rainfall zones. The hard seeded variety Prolific Persian clover is an early flowering option selected on the basis of early seedling vigour and its hard seededness for Western Australian conditions.
details.grazingManagementNotes: Regrowth after grazing is excellent and it has as high a nutritive value as pasture or hay. Hard seeded Persian clover is well suited to rotational grazing systems sown with other annual legumes and ryegrass.

products.name: Prima Gland Clover
products.descriptionSource: Rewritten from live website page text

details.blurb: Whiteseeded type. Early maturing with good regenerative abilities. Tolerant of Red Legged Earth Mite and Blue Green Aphid.
details.notes: [2026 guide] 2026 guide sowing rate is 4 to 6 kg/ha; this row records 'Single species: 5 to 7kg/ha; Mixes: 1 - 2kg/ha' — reconcile. 2026 guide rainfall is 350mm+; this row records '300mm+ - 600mm' — reconcile.
details.tagline: Early maturing, pest tolerant
details.description:
Prima is a gland clover, an aerial seeding, self-regenerating annual legume that forms dense, extensively branched swards. It occupies a useful position: adaptable across a wide range of soil types while being genuinely suited to low rainfall environments.

Its most valuable characteristic is insect tolerance. Prima is resistant to red-legged earth mite, blue-green aphid and cowpea aphid, three of the pests that most reliably damage establishing legumes, and that resistance reduces both the risk of a failed establishment and the cost of controlling it. It is moderately susceptible to spotted alfalfa aphid and lucerne flea.

It is early maturing and hard seeded, which together give it excellent regeneration, and it will take mildly waterlogged soils though not infertile sands. Light frosts to around minus four or five degrees are tolerated.

The seed is easy to harvest for conservation, which makes it practical for growers producing their own. Prima produces high quality forage in terms of protein, digestibility and energy, though quality declines with age and it is only moderately palatable, so it is best used before it becomes rank.

Resistant to red-legged earth mite and aphids

products.name: Red Clover
products.descriptionSource: Rewritten from master catalogue tech sheets

details.blurb: A late flowering, summer active highly productive perennial legume with high feed value. Suitable for grazing, silage or hay. It has a strong tap root, has some drought tolerance and good summer growth. Often sown as a component in a mix for permanent pasture.
details.notes: NEW ROW (added from the 2026 guide). Not previously in the catalogue in any form. No tech sheet located in the source library.
details.tagline: Good summer growth, tap rooted, drought tolerant
details.description:
Red clover is a perennial legume grown for summer production, and it fills a gap that most pasture legumes leave open.

Its deep taproot is the reason. Where white clover is shallow rooted and shuts down as the topsoil dries, red clover reaches moisture further down and keeps growing into summer, so a pasture carrying it produces feed in the period when a grass-and-white-clover sward has stopped. That same taproot gives it real drought tolerance.

The forage is high quality for both grazing and hay, and the plant fixes nitrogen strongly, which benefits the grass component of the pasture and the crop that follows.

Red clover suits medium to high rainfall pasture, sown with perennial ryegrass, fescue or a herb component, where the aim is a longer feed curve across the year rather than maximum winter bulk. It is generally shorter lived than white clover under hard grazing, so it is best managed with recovery periods that let the crown rebuild.
details.botanicalName: Trifolium pratense (inferred from species, not stated in the guide)
keyAttributes: Good summer growth from a deep taproot
High quality forage for grazing and hay
Suits medium to high rainfall pasture

products.name: Riverina Subterranean Clover
products.descriptionSource: Rewritten from live website page text

details.blurb: A white seeded, (Yanninicum) type, with mid season maturity exhibiting high forage production with good levels of hard seed. Increased autumn and winter production over Trikkala. Riverina withstands waterlogging and has high levels of resistance to Phytophthora Root Rot, Scorch and Powdery Mildew.
details.notes: [2026 guide] 2026 guide rainfall is 425mm+; this row records '450mm+' — reconcile.
details.tagline: Higher production than older varieties, handles wet
details.description:
Riverina is a subterranean clover of the yanninicum group, bred for waterlogging tolerant country and positioned between Trikkala and Gosse in maturity. At Perth it flowers at 119 days, against Trikkala at 112 and Gosse at 126.

Its advantages over both are specific. It produces more feed through early and mid winter than Gosse, which is the part of the season where a legume contributes most to carrying capacity. And it carries a higher hard seed content than either Trikkala or Gosse, which is the trait that determines whether a stand comes back after a cropping phase, since Trikkala in particular is soft seeded and regenerates poorly.

It also carries lower levels of the oestrogenic isoflavone formononetin than Trikkala, which matters where ewes are joined on clover-dominant pasture.

Riverina suits early watering programmes and tolerates some waterlogging, making it a good fit for irrigated country and heavier flats where a productive, reliably regenerating sub clover is wanted.
details.bredByOrigin: Bred by Dr J S Gladstones, University of WA; derived from the same cross as Gosse (Meteora/Trikkala)
keyAttributes: Increased early to mid winter production
Higher hard seed content than Trikkala and Gosse
details.seoDescription: Riverina belongs to the water logging tolerant subspecies yanninicum of sub clover, and is derived from the same cross as Gosse, (Meteora/Trikkala). and was bred by Dr J S Gladstones from the University of WA.
details.standLifeNotes: Higher hard seed content than Trikkala and Gosse. The higher levels of hard seediness will increase the potential of increased production in the following years.
details.diseasePestResistance: Resistant to Race 1 and at least moderately resistant to Race 2 clover scorch; lower formononetin than Trikkala; higher tolerance to leaf rust and leaf spot; more resistance to powdery mildew than Gosse

details.tagline: Older variety with good production
details.description:
Seaton Park is an early to mid season subterranean clover that has been sown across Western Australia for long enough to be a known quantity, and it remains a dependable choice in mixed farming rotations.

Its maturity places it between the very early varieties bred for the driest country and the mid to late types that need a longer season, which makes it broadly useful across the medium rainfall zone rather than specialised to one district.

Production is good and regeneration is reliable, which is what a rotation legume is asked to do: fix nitrogen, provide winter and spring feed, and come back after the paddock has been cropped without needing to be resown.

Newer varieties out-perform it on specific traits, particularly disease resistance and hard seed levels, and growers replacing an old stand should look at what has been released since. But as a widely proven, well understood sub clover, Seaton Park continues to earn its place, particularly where seed availability and cost matter.
keyAttributes: Long established sub clover across WA
details.seoDescription: Seaton Park is a black seeded mid-season flowering subterranean clover that is very persistent even under heavy grazing and/or low rainfall.

Produces lower levels of hard seed (+/- 23%) compared to Urana and Dalkeith. Insufficient hard seededness for reliable persistence in tight cropping rotations (1year crop:1year pasture).

details.tagline: Tolerant of seasonal flooding
details.description:
Shaftal is a late flowering Persian clover with large leaves and an erect habit, grown for high quality feed on wet country and for its ability to be cut more than once.

It is highly nutritive for sheep and cattle and productive right through autumn, winter and spring, which is a longer productive run than most annual legumes manage. Its erect growth makes it straightforward to cut, and as a multi-cut crop it suits pasture, hay and silage from the same stand, with good regrowth after each grazing or cut.

Waterlogging tolerance is excellent and salt tolerance is moderate, so it performs on flats and heavier ground that would defeat a sub clover.

Shaftal is non-oestrogenic, meaning it will not cause infertility or reproductive disorders in ewes, which removes a real constraint when joining stock on clover-dominant pasture.

It works particularly well in short term ryegrass mixes, where its late flowering complements the grass and extends the quality of the conserved feed. Being soft seeded, it is sown for the season rather than relied on to regenerate.

products.descriptionSource: Rewritten from live website page text

details.blurb: Perennial clover suited to waterlogged areas, tolerant to mild salinity and neutral to alkaline soils. Grazing tolerant and persistent. More productive through spring and summer than winter. Can cause bloat in cattle.

details.tagline: Perennial clover for wet, mildly saline ground
details.description:
Strawberry clover is a deep rooted, prostrate perennial clover for country that is wet, mildly saline, or both, and it is one of the more durable legumes available for that ground.

It is palatable with high protein content, productive through spring and summer rather than winter, and it tolerates heavy grazing while remaining persistent. That grazing tolerance comes from its prostrate habit: growing points sit below the grazing height, so the plant is not removed by hard stocking the way an erect legume would be.

It is drought resistant thanks to its depth of root, waterlogging tolerant, and moderately salt tolerant, which is an unusual combination and the reason it appears on saltland and seasonally flooded flats.

Strawberry clover is free of oestrogen risks, so it can be grazed by breeding ewes without concern.

It performs best on neutral to alkaline soils and is long season and hard seeded, sown with grasses such as tall fescue, tall wheat grass, puccinellia or phalaris to build a durable pasture on difficult country.

products.name: Tribute White Clover
products.descriptionSource: Rewritten from master catalogue tech sheets

details.blurb: A medium to large leaved white clover with strong persistence, superior out-of-season production and very high dry matter yields. Tribute has a superior stolon density to leaf size ratio, tolerance of clover root weevil, and stays persistent under hard grazing. It is adaptable across a wide range of farm types and suits all grazing regimes.
details.tagline: Persistent white clover with high year-round yield
details.description:
Tribute is a medium to large leaved white clover selected for persistence and for production outside the main growing season, which is where most white clovers disappoint.

Its key structural trait is a superior ratio of stolon density to leaf size. White clover survives by its stolons, the runners that spread across the ground and root down, and a large leaved clover with sparse stolons will yield well and then thin out under grazing. Tribute carries the leaf size for yield and the stolon density for survival, which is why it stays persistent under hard grazing where larger leaved types fail.

It also tolerates clover root weevil, a pest that can progressively destroy a white clover stand, and it delivers very high dry matter production year-round with superior out-of-season growth.

Tribute is adaptable across a wide range of farm types and suits all grazing regimes, from set stocking through to intensive rotation. In a high performance pasture it is the white clover to reach for first, sown with perennial ryegrass, fescue or herbs.

High stolon density to leaf size ratio

products.name: Trikkala Sub Clover
products.descriptionSource: Rewritten from master catalogue tech sheets

details.blurb: A white seeded, mid-maturing sub clover that is prostrate, self-regenerating and tolerant of both waterlogging and heavy grazing. Trikkala suits medium to heavy acidic soils receiving at least 450mm a year, and performs well on flood plains and in irrigated environments. It is a soft seeded variety with vigorous seedlings that provide good winter feed.

The contaminated trailing figures were NOT used; the internally-consistent body-text figures were used instead.
details.tagline: Mid-maturing clover tolerant of waterlogging
details.description:
Trikkala is a white seeded, mid-maturing subterranean clover of the yanninicum group, and for many years it was the standard choice for waterlogged country.

It is a prostrate, self-regenerating annual that grows from autumn through to spring and buries its burrs, and it tolerates both waterlogging and heavy grazing. It performs particularly well on flood plains and in irrigated environments, and it is adapted to soils prone to winter waterlogging that would defeat most sub clovers.

Its seedlings are vigorous and provide good winter feed, and it shows good winter and early spring vigour generally. It is very persistent in high rainfall areas.

The limitation is its seed. Trikkala is soft seeded with very low levels of hard seed, so while it regenerates well in a permanent pasture where it sets seed each year, it does not hold a reserve in the soil through a cropping phase. Growers wanting a yanninicum type for a crop rotation should consider Gosse or Riverina, both of which were developed with higher hard seed for that reason.

Vigorous seedlings provide good winter feed
Very persistent in high rainfall areas
Adapted to soils prone to winter waterlogging
Performs well on flood plains and irrigation

The limitations of Trikkala is that it has poor persistence on well-drained sandy soils. It has insufficient hard seededness for persistence in tight cropping rotations such as 1 year crop; 1 year pasture.

products.name: Urana Subterranean Clover
products.descriptionSource: Rewritten from live website page text

details.blurb: Urana is a highly winter-active, high-producing sub clover with strong hard-seed levels and low formononetin. Urana’s indeterminate nature allows it to keep growing right through into spring when moisture is available. Urana performs best in well-drained, higher-rainfall areas, where it delivers outstanding winter production.
details.tagline: Increased winter and spring production, harder seed
details.description:
Urana is a subterranean clover selected for winter activity, and it is described as the most winter active sub clover yet seen in the trials it came through, which translates directly into increased returns per hectare.

Winter activity is where a pasture legume adds the most value. Feed grown in winter is the feed a farm would otherwise have to buy, so a clover that produces when others are dormant lifts carrying capacity at the point of greatest cost.

It flowers slightly later than Dalkeith but earlier than Seaton Park, at around 103 days at Perth, and it has the capacity to produce greater total herbage than other cultivars. It also carries higher levels of hard seed than Dalkeith, which should allow it to persist well through cropping rotations, and that combination of production and persistence is what suits it to a pasture phase between crops.

It is susceptible to race 1 clover scorch but moderately resistant to race 2, so its fit depends on which races are present in the district.
