products.name: Amplify Phalaris
products.descriptionSource: Rewritten from live website page text

details.blurb: A great all rounder with high winter forage yields and some summer production under favourable conditions. Can go summer dormant under adverse conditions for increased persistence. A long term perennial that has increased seedling vigour and lower toxicity. Tolerance to acid soils and heavy grazing.
details.tagline: Deep rooted perennial tolerating waterlogging and salt
details.description:
Amplify is a phalaris, and phalaris occupies a particular place in Australian pasture: a deep rooted perennial grass that survives conditions which finish off perennial ryegrass, and then persists for many years once established.

Its value is in that durability. A phalaris stand is slow to establish compared with a ryegrass, but once the root system is down it tolerates drought, waterlogging and salinity, and it holds the paddock through seasons that would require a ryegrass pasture to be resown.

Amplify produces strongly through winter and spring, which is when most of the year's feed is grown in a Mediterranean system, and its tolerance of wet and saline ground makes it a genuine option for heavier soils and flats where the alternatives are limited.

It suits producers taking a long view of a paddock, sown with a companion legume so the pasture has a nitrogen source, and managed to let the crown establish properly in the first year before it is grazed hard.
details.seoDescription: Phalaris has been one of Australia’s success stories for temperate grasses. Up until recently, it was the only grass that had its own long-term breeding program. Australia has been the leader in Phalaris aquatica variety development and it is well suited to the southern Australian environment with it being the…
details.standLifeNotes: Long-term perennial; can go summer dormant under adverse conditions for increased persistence (stated)
details.grazingManagementNotes: Phalaris is slow to establish and should be given plenty of time. Only very light grazing recommended in the first year to encourage tillering; grazing should otherwise be avoided in year one, especially during flowering, when dormant buds form for long-term persistence. Achieve Diploid Italian Ryegrass will produce high quality grazing and silage and, where managed appropriately, can provide excellent high-quality pasture for up to two years.

products.name: Anywhere Tall Fescue
products.descriptionSource: Rewritten from live website page text

details.blurb: An Australian bred and grown Mediterranean fescue selected for increased seedling vigour, letting plants establish before soil temperatures drop and weed competition sets in. Anywhere has a later heading date than other Mediterranean tall fescues, so feed quality is retained longer. As a winter active hybrid type it allows some summer growth if rains occur, and goes summer dormant if they do not.
details.tagline: Australian bred winter active Mediterranean fescue
details.description:
Anywhere is an Australian bred and grown Mediterranean tall fescue, developed around a specific establishment problem. Mediterranean fescues are valuable because they go dormant through summer and survive where continental types die, but they have traditionally been slow to establish, which leaves the seedling exposed to falling soil temperatures and to weed competition before it is strong enough to compete.

Anywhere was selected for increased seedling vigour to close that window. Getting established before the soil cools and before weeds take hold is the difference between a stand that persists and one that has to be resown.

It also carries a later heading date than other Mediterranean tall fescues, which allows feed quality to be retained longer into the season rather than the sward running to stem early.

As a winter active Mediterranean hybrid type it will grow through summer if rain arrives, and go dormant if it does not, which is exactly the behaviour wanted in country with unreliable summer rainfall. It has broad, long leaves and produces across the seasons in both wet and dry years.
details.bredByOrigin: Australian bred and grown (specific breeder company not named)

Increased seedling vigour for fast establishment
Later heading retains feed quality longer
Winter active with summer dormancy in dry years
Some summer growth when rains arrive

products.name: Atom Prairie Grass
products.descriptionSource: Rewritten from master catalogue tech sheets

details.blurb: An alternative short to long rotation option where high quality feed is the priority. Atom is nil endophyte with palatable seed heads, high protein and good summer heat tolerance, making it a strong fit for finishing young stock through late spring, summer and autumn. It also produces well in winter, similar to short rotation ryegrasses, and is friendly to clovers and herbs.
details.notes: ⚠ The flyer file is branded "Another great product from: [Agricom]" (agricom.com.au) and lists third-party distributors — Stephen Pasture Seeds (VIC/SA/TAS), AusWest Seeds (NSW/QLD), Smyth Seeds (VIC/NSW) — with no mention of IH Seeds/Irwin Hunter at all. Douglas should confirm whether IH Seeds is an authorised reseller of this Agricom-bred variety or whether this flyer was just used as a generic content source.
details.tagline: High quality winter forage with palatable seedheads
details.description:
Atom is a prairie grass, offering an alternative to ryegrass where high quality feed is the priority and where summer heat limits what a ryegrass can do.

It is nil endophyte, which means no risk of the alkaloid-related animal health problems associated with endophyte-carrying ryegrasses, and that makes it particularly suitable for finishing young stock where growth rates matter and any check to intake is costly.

Its seedhead is palatable, which is unusual and useful: most grasses lose intake sharply once they run to head, whereas stock will keep eating a prairie grass through that stage. Protein content is high, and the species is friendly to clovers and herbs, so it sits well in a diverse sward rather than dominating it.

Summer heat tolerance combined with good winter production, similar to short rotation ryegrasses, gives it an unusually long useful season. Atom therefore works as either a short or long rotation option, and suits late spring, summer and autumn finishing of young cattle as well as hay.
details.bredByOrigin: Agricom (per flyer branding — "Another great product from:" / agricom.com.au; not credited as breeder in IH Seeds' own tech sheets)
keyAttributes: Summer heat tolerance for finishing stock
Good option for cattle grazing and hay
details.standLifeNotes: Bromes have the potential to persist for longer than ryegrass in subtropical pastures, particularly benefiting northern Australia (stated). Longer grazing intervals during late spring and summer are essential for prairie grass persistence and reseeding.

Graze once plant reaches 4 tillers; mid-winter grazing interval 30-35 days, early spring 20-25 days; longer intervals in late spring/summer allow lower tillers to senesce and form a protective mat. Cattle grazing and hay option. There are three major brome species in commercial use; Prairie Grass, Pasture Brome, and Grazing Brome. Establishment and Grazing Management.

details.tagline: Winter active Mediterranean, extremely drought tolerant
details.description:
Flecha is a highly winter active Mediterranean tall fescue selected for drought tolerance and persistence, and it carries the Max P endophyte.

As a Mediterranean type it is dormant through summer, which is the mechanism behind its drought survival: rather than trying to grow through heat and dry, the plant shuts down, conserves its crown, and recovers quickly in autumn to produce large amounts of forage through autumn, winter and spring. In country with hot dry summers that strategy outlasts a continental grass trying to stay active.

The Max P endophyte provides high insect resistance without the animal health problems associated with wild-type endophytes, which is what allows a persistent fescue to be grazed safely.

Establishment vigour is good, and the leaves are fine, soft and palatable, addressing the traditional objection to tall fescue that stock will not eat it readily. It suits a wide range of soil types.

Flecha is for producers wanting a perennial that will still be there after a run of dry years.

details.tagline: Summer active fescue for heavy, wet and saline soils
details.description:
Hummer is a summer active tall fescue that yields across all four seasons, developed for farms wanting a perennial that keeps producing where perennial ryegrass runs into trouble.

It tolerates heavy, wet and moderately saline soils better than perennial ryegrass, and it carries better heat tolerance, summer productivity and summer feed quality, while using water more efficiently under irrigation. That combination is what makes it a genuine alternative rather than a fallback on difficult country.

Structurally it is soft leaved and fine tillered with a sod forming habit, and the sod forming trait matters most for persistence: over time it builds dense crowns that hold the paddock rather than opening up. It is deep rooted, with a large coarse fibrous root mass often found well below the rooting depth of perennial ryegrass, which underpins both its drought tolerance and its natural tolerance of grass grub. The Max P endophyte extends insect tolerance further.

Its early heading gives strong late winter and early spring growth, and the fine soft leaves encourage grazing and lift utilisation, so the pasture remains palatable beyond its optimum grazing height.

details.tagline: High quality feed with all year round production
details.description:
Matua is a prairie grass, a short-lived perennial grown for feed quality rather than sheer bulk, and particularly for what it does in the months when a ryegrass pasture has lost its edge.

It is a highly palatable cool season grass that maintains quality through hot months, which is the trait that distinguishes it. Most cool season grasses become stemmy and unpalatable as temperatures rise; Matua holds together well enough to keep intake up.

It reseeds itself each growth period, which extends stand life beyond what a short-lived perennial would otherwise deliver, provided it is managed to allow seed set. That self-reseeding is the mechanism by which a prairie grass paddock persists.

Protein content is high, and it is friendly to clovers and herbs, so it works in a diverse sward rather than crowding companions out.

Matua suits producers finishing stock, or anyone wanting year round production with an emphasis on quality, and it is best established as the sole grass in a mix so it is not out-competed early.

Strict rotational grazing/harvest only after boot or early seed stage; 25-35 day rest period (faster in cool periods, slower in summer); will not tolerate continuous grazing or wet/muddy conditions. Must be rotationally grazed for good production and persistence. There are three major brome species in commercial use; Prairie Grass, Pasture Brome, and Grazing Brome. Establishment and Grazing Management. A rest period of 25-35 days is required between grazing/harvests depending on the time of the year.

details.tagline: Perennial option for sandy soils
details.description:
Mission veldt grass is a perennial for sandy country, and it is one of relatively few perennial grasses that will persist on genuinely poor sands without substantial fertiliser inputs.

It establishes readily, which is not a given on light soils where moisture drains away quickly and seedlings can be lost. Once established it is long-lived, drought tolerant, and it produces useful early winter growth, filling the part of the season when annual pastures have not yet got going.

That early growth is the practical case for it. On sandplain country running annual pasture, the autumn to early winter period is the tightest, and a perennial that is already established and responds to the first rains carries stock through it.

Mission suits sheep grazing systems on light land, sown with a hard seeded legume so the pasture has a nitrogen source. It is not a high production grass in absolute terms, and it is not intended to be; its value is persistence and reliability on country that will not support anything more demanding.
details.seoDescription: Mission Veldt grass is a fine-stemmed, densely tufted perennial bunchgrass that has been selected for use on light sandy soils and is especially good for erosion control.
details.standLifeNotes: Easily established, long-lived variety (stated)
details.grazingManagementNotes: Watch young seedlings for insect attack; seedlings do not compete well with Capeweed and annual grasses. Farmers should check test results (seed content, germination, weed content) since unselected wild veldt grass seed sheds too freely to harvest reliably.

products.name: Puccinellia
products.descriptionSource: Rewritten from live website page text

details.tagline: Low input winter active pasture for saline, wet ground
details.description:
Puccinellia is a winter active perennial grass for saltland, and it tolerates salinity that would kill almost anything else grown as pasture.

It is used where land has gone out of production through salinity and waterlogging, and where the realistic choice is between bare, scalded ground and a low input perennial that will hold the soil and produce some feed. Puccinellia does the second.

Being winter active, it grows when the topsoil is least saline. Salt concentrates at the surface over summer as water evaporates, and winter rain flushes it down, so a grass that produces in the cool wet months is working in the window when conditions are most favourable.

It requires minimal fertiliser input, which is appropriate given the country it is asked to grow on, and it handles waterlogged ground as well as salt.

Puccinellia is usually sown alongside tall wheat grass and a salt tolerant legume such as strawberry clover or messina, so that different parts of a variable saline paddock are each occupied by the species best suited to them.
details.seoDescription: Puccinellia is a perennial grass that is tolerant to both salinity and water logging, although it is sensitive to water logged soils during establishment and requires a dry soil surface during summer.
details.standLifeNotes: Ready to graze only in the second year after planting; responds quickly to opening rains and thrives in winter/spring flooding conditions (stated)
details.diseasePestResistance: Susceptible to red-legged earth mite at establishment (stated); no noted livestock disorder or toxicity (stated)
details.grazingManagementNotes: Sow autumn to early winter, shallow due to small seed. Select paddocks free of barley grass at establishment. Flowers September-November; seed harvested over summer. Puccinellia is ready to graze in the second year after planting during the late autumn and winter however avoid overgrazing in the spring as this can significantly reduce ground cover and plant numbers through pulling, especially where grazed with sheep.

details.blurb: A vigorous, very high yielding perennial cocksfoot that produces well all year round while holding summer quality and palatability. Unlike most cocksfoot varieties Savvy has a late heading date and exceptionally low aftermath heading, with soft leaves and a very short period of seed head development. That makes it relatively easy to manage, particularly with cattle.

details.tagline: High yielding cocksfoot with low aftermath heading
details.description:
Savvy is a vigorous, very high yielding perennial cocksfoot, and it was developed to fix the reason many producers avoid cocksfoot altogether: it becomes coarse and unpalatable once it heads.

Savvy has a late heading date, unusual among cocksfoots, and exceptionally low aftermath heading, meaning the period of seed head development is very short and few heads appear between grazings. It is also an indiscriminate seeder, so under grazing many plants produce no seed head at all. The practical result is a sward that stays leafy and palatable through the season instead of turning stemmy.

Combined with soft leaves, that makes it relatively easy to manage, particularly with cattle, which are less able than sheep to select leaf out of a stemmy sward.

Production is high all year round, and summer quality and palatability are maintained rather than collapsing. Savvy suits producers who want the drought tolerance and persistence of a cocksfoot without the management difficulty that older varieties brought with them.

details.tagline: Will survive and thrive through tough conditions
details.description:
Tall fescue is a deep rooted perennial grass grown where conditions are too hard, too wet or too hot for perennial ryegrass to persist, and it is one of the most durable pasture grasses available.

Its root system is the reason. Tall fescue roots deeper than ryegrass, reaching moisture and nutrients beyond ryegrass's range, which is what allows it to survive dry summers and to keep producing when a ryegrass pasture has shut down. The same root mass handles heavy and wet soils that would rot out a shallower rooted species.

As a perennial base it holds a paddock across years rather than seasons, and it suits all classes of grazing livestock.

The trade-off with fescue has always been palatability, since older types were coarse and stock ate them reluctantly. Modern soft-leaved varieties have largely addressed this, and where a named variety is available it is generally the better choice. Generic tall fescue remains a cost effective option for bulk, durability and erosion control on country that needs covering.

products.descriptionSource: Rewritten from live website page text

details.blurb: Later maturing perennial adapted to a wide range of soil types including poorly drained and saline effected areas. It has high salt tolerance and will grow and persist in highly alkaline soils. Can be sown into saline areas with between 3 to 5dS/m (Deci siemens per metre). Can also be used in reclamation of saline soils and for soil conservation; also for pasture in low rainfall, non saline soils. Ideal companion to Puccinellia.
details.tagline: Best pasture option for saline and waterlogged areas
details.description:
Tyrrell is a tall wheat grass, and it is the standard choice for the most difficult saline and waterlogged country in a pasture programme.

Tall wheat grass tolerates salinity levels and prolonged waterlogging that exclude nearly every other productive pasture species, and it does so as a deep rooted, very persistent perennial. On saltland it is often the species that makes the difference between land producing something and producing nothing.

It generates substantial bulk on marginal country, which is useful both as feed and as ground cover, and it is widely used for saltland reclamation, where a deep rooted perennial lowers the water table locally and slows the movement of salt back to the surface.

Tyrrell is coarse, and stock will graze it more readily when it is kept young rather than allowed to run up, so it responds to management. It is typically sown with puccinellia and a salt tolerant legume so that the range of conditions across a saline paddock is covered.

details.tagline: Soft, palatable fescue with ryegrass-like appeal
details.description:
Tower is a summer active tall fescue produced in New Zealand, and it was developed to overcome the negative features of older tall fescues while offering more than perennial ryegrass can.

The traditional objection to fescue is palatability, and Tower answers it directly: it is a soft, palatable grass which animals preferred over ryegrass at trial sites. That preference is the whole argument for it. A grass stock choose to eat is easier to manage, gets utilised properly rather than being left to go rank, and delivers better animal performance in beef cattle, lambs and dairy cows.

Alongside that it brings what a fescue is normally chosen for: much better drought tolerance and persistence than perennial ryegrass, and strong autumn and winter recovery.

Tower is for producers who would like the durability of a fescue but have been put off by how earlier types grazed. It suits summer rainfall and irrigated country, and it persists in situations where a perennial ryegrass stand would need replacing.

details.tagline: Persistent, high yielding, cold and drought tolerant
details.description:
Treposno is a persistent, high yielding perennial cocksfoot, and it is chosen for country where cold and drought both need to be survived in the same paddock.

Cocksfoot as a species is deep rooted and tolerant of low fertility, which is why it persists on hillsides and lighter soils that will not carry a perennial ryegrass. Treposno carries that with tolerance of both cold and drought, an unusual pairing that suits districts with cold winters and dry summers rather than one or the other.

Its deep root system is what gets it through summer, drawing on moisture below the reach of shallower rooted grasses and allowing the crown to survive until the autumn break.

Stand life under grazing is long, which is the main reason to choose a cocksfoot in the first place. Treposno suits lower fertility country being managed for the long term, sown with a companion legume, and grazed to keep it leafy rather than allowed to become stemmy.

details.tagline: Fine leaved, drought and cold tolerant cocksfoot
details.description:
Uplands is a fine leaved Mediterranean cocksfoot with high tiller density, developed for low rainfall temperate country where drought and cold both limit what can be grown.

Its drought and cold tolerance are both described as very high, and as a winter active, partially summer dormant type it follows the Mediterranean strategy: grow hard through the cool season, shut down through summer, and survive rather than exhaust itself trying to produce in heat. That is what allows it to persist in country too dry for most perennials.

Fine leaves and high tiller density are what make it palatable and productive rather than coarse, and it produces a large bulk of high protein, high energy forage that stock take readily.

It is very tolerant of aluminium and acid soils, which considerably widens the country it can be sown on, since acidity limits root growth for many species.

Uplands grows rapidly from autumn to late spring and persists well under grazing, suiting sheep and cattle systems on low rainfall temperate land.

details.tagline: Softer leaved Porto selection for 450mm+ zones
details.description:
Yarck is a selection from Porto type cocksfoots, developed to improve on them in the traits that matter most in a grazing system.

Porto types are widely used and durable, but they are coarse and their production is concentrated later. Yarck is a medium flowering type carrying increased dry matter production through winter and early spring compared with Porto, which shifts feed into the part of the season when it is most valuable. Its leaves are softer, which lifts palatability and therefore utilisation.

It also improves on Porto in persistence, with increased seedling vigour giving better establishment, and establishment is where a cocksfoot stand is most often lost.

Where it is sown into higher rainfall zones, Yarck can respond to summer rainfall rather than remaining dormant, which extends its useful season.

It suits the medium to higher rainfall parts of the state, sown with other perennial species and a companion legume to build a pasture that produces across the whole year rather than in a single flush.

products.name: Cadiz Serradella
products.descriptionSource: Rewritten from DPIRD / Agriculture WA publication

details.blurb: The first variety of French serradella to be developed in Australia, released for the 1996 season and bred for low fertility, acid soils where subterranean clover has failed. Cadiz is soft seeded, so it germinates readily without de-hulling and regenerates strongly in its second season at much higher densities than the hard seeded yellow serradellas. On poor acid sands it can lift carrying capacity from around 1 to 5 DSE/ha.

details.tagline: Soft seeded serradella for deep acid sands
details.description:
Cadiz was the first French serradella developed in Australia, released for the 1996 growing season out of work by CLIMA and the Pasture Improvement Group at Agriculture Western Australia. The problem it was bred to solve was a specific one: large areas of the West Midlands carry deep, infertile acid sands where subterranean clover simply will not persist, leaving country running at little more than one dry sheep equivalent per hectare.

What made Cadiz different was its soft seed. Where the hard-seeded yellow serradellas need de-hulling and take several seasons to build a stand, Cadiz germinates readily from pod and comes back in its second season at far higher densities. Growers can lift stock numbers from year two rather than waiting, and on the poorest acid sands the gain in carrying capacity has been measured at around fivefold.

Being deep rooted, it also asks less of the paddock than shallower rooted legumes, needing less phosphorus and potassium for good growth while returning nitrogen and organic matter to soils usually short of both. It suits the sheep and mixed farming country of the northern and central wheatbelt.

The soft seed is also the catch. Cadiz will not regenerate after a cropping phase, so it belongs in a pasture phase rather than a tight crop rotation unless it is sown alongside a hard seeded variety.

details.tagline: Spineless burr with waterlogging and salinity tolerance
details.description:
Cavalier is a spineless burr medic, and both halves of that description matter. Burr medics are annual pasture legumes for neutral to alkaline soils in the mixed farming zone; the spineless trait removes the burr's hooked spines, which otherwise contaminate wool and make seed harvesting difficult.

It is more acid tolerant than the barrel and strand medics, which extends its range onto country those species cannot handle, and it offers good waterlogging and salinity tolerance alongside that, so it suits variable paddocks rather than only the best ground.

Nutritionally it is a high protein annual legume, palatable at all growth stages including senesced dry matter and seed pods over summer, so it continues to contribute feed after it has finished growing. That summer contribution is often overlooked and is one of the real advantages of a medic in a mixed farming system.

Where effectively nodulated it fixes atmospheric nitrogen, benefiting the cereal crop grown in rotation after it, and as a grass-free legume phase it also functions as a disease break. Cavalier replaced Santiago on the strength of superior dry matter production.

details.tagline: Fast growing hard seeded barrel medic that holds its pod
details.description:
Cheetah is an early to mid maturing barrel medic bred for low to medium rainfall country, and it is highly vigorous, fast growing and drought tolerant.

Its stand-out feature is the pod holding trait. Most medics drop their maturing pods and leaves as the plant dries off, which puts the seed on the ground where it is exposed to weather and to grazing, and takes the dry residue out of reach as summer feed. Cheetah holds its pods and leaves on the plant, so the feed stays available to stock into summer and the seed is retained where it can be harvested or grazed deliberately.

It carries multiple aphid resistances, which protects both establishment and production in districts where aphid pressure is a recurring problem, and it is hard seeded, giving reliable regeneration from the soil seed bank through a cropping rotation.

Cheetah performs on neutral and alkaline loams and clays in the drier parts of the mixed farming zone, and its early flowering means it completes seed set before the season closes.

Eliza is a soft seeded French serradella with pink flowers and a segmented pod, developed as an improvement on Cadiz.

details.tagline: Prolific seeder that handles heavy grazing
details.description:
Santiago is a spineless burr medic collected in Chile and introduced to Australia in 1981. It is early to mid maturing, flowering eighty days after seeding, with a smooth burr pod that avoids the wool contamination and harvesting problems caused by spiny types.

It is a prolific seeder, and that is the basis of its persistence: a heavy seed set builds a soil seed bank that carries the pasture through cropping phases and across seasons. It tolerates a wide range of soil types and pH ranges, and it is very tolerant of heavy grazing, which is unusual and useful in a legume expected to survive in a grazed rotation.

As an annual pasture legume it is palatable at all growth stages, including senesced dry matter and seed pods over summer, so it keeps contributing feed after it has finished growing. Nutritive value is high with high protein content, and where effectively nodulated it fixes nitrogen that benefits the cereal crop grown after it.

Santiago has since been superseded by Cavalier, which produces more dry matter, though Santiago remains widely adapted and dependable.

details.tagline: High performing hard seeded yellow serradella
details.description:
Santorini is a hard seeded yellow serradella bred for acidic sandy loam soils, with an upright growth habit and early maturity, flowering at approximately 100 days from sowing at Perth.

Its upright habit is a practical advantage. It offers easy grazing access for stock, so the feed on offer is actually harvested rather than left below grazing height, and it makes seed harvest more straightforward.

The increased hard seededness gives increased persistence, and as with the other hard seeded serradellas that persistence compounds into greater total dry matter production across an extended pasture phase and greater nitrogen generation for the following crop.

An unusual feature is its prolonged germination period, spread over roughly forty days. That spread is a form of insurance: rather than committing every seedling to a single germinating rain, the stand emerges in waves, so a false break destroys only part of the cohort.

It is compatible with group S inoculant and suits the acid sandplain country where sub clover and medic will not persist.

details.tagline: Hard seeded and highly regenerative
details.description:
Serramax is a hard seeded serradella selected for regeneration, and it is aimed squarely at cropping rotations on acid sandy country.

Serradellas earn their place on soils too acid and too infertile for sub clover, where they fix nitrogen and produce feed that would otherwise be unavailable. The limitation of the soft seeded types is that they cannot survive a cropping phase, because their seed germinates rather than waiting. Serramax is hard seeded and highly regenerative, so the soil seed bank persists through the crop and the pasture returns without resowing.

It is deep rooted, which underpins its drought tolerance and lets it draw on subsoil moisture late in the season, and it fixes nitrogen strongly for the benefit of the crop that follows.

Serramax suits acid sandplain in a mixed farming rotation, where the pasture phase has to pay its way both in livestock production and in nitrogen left behind for the cereal crop.

details.tagline: Vigorous mid-late sub clover with mite tolerance
details.description:
SF Narrikup is a very vigorous mid to late season subterranean clover of the subterraneum group, and it was released in Australia in 2013 to address a problem that had been costing growers money at establishment.

Emerging sub clover seedlings are highly vulnerable to red-legged earth mite, and the standard answer has been insecticide. SF Narrikup's seedlings suffer less damage from mite than older subterraneum clovers, which improves establishment and lifts first year yields, and it reduces the need for insecticide and the cost of applying it. It also produces heavily in winter, driven by strong seedling regeneration, and winter is where a pasture legume contributes most to carrying capacity.

SF Narrikup suits well drained, moderately acid soils in southern Australia where the growing season extends to mid-November, and it is suitable for all livestock types as well as silage and hay. It out-produces Campeda substantially in winter and spring, and out-performs Junee in winter.

details.tagline: Winter active lucerne with a high leaf to stem ratio
alsoKnownAs: SGI Alpha-1 Lucerne – The King of Forage.
details.description:
Alpha 1 is a highly winter active lucerne bred from Australian, American and Argentinian germplasm, selected for increased winter activity, fast establishment and finer stems with a high leaf to stem ratio.

That leaf to stem ratio is the trait doing most of the work. Leaf carries the protein and the digestibility in a lucerne stand; stem carries fibre. A variety with finer stems and proportionally more leaf therefore produces higher quality feed from the same tonnage, which shows up in both hay quality and animal performance.

Winter activity is the other half. A highly winter active lucerne keeps producing through the cool months rather than going dormant, extending the feed curve at the time of year when feed is scarcest.

Alpha 1 shows strong autumn and winter to spring growth with vigorous recovery from cutting or grazing, and that recovery is what makes it suitable for close grazed pastures and intensive forage cutting programmes where the stand is asked to come back repeatedly.

Improved disease and insect resistance underpins the stand life needed to justify the establishment cost.

details.blurb: Developed by selection from old established lucerne stands where high plant populations had survived over time, with selection based on superior forage yields and improved disease and pest tolerance. Icon plants are moderately tall with leafy stems and a high leaf to stem ratio. With a winter activity rating of 6 to 7 it grows well through winter, spring and summer where moisture is available, and performs in sites where disease susceptible varieties will not persist.

details.tagline: Winter active 6-7 with strong disease resistance
details.description:
Icon was developed by selection from old established lucerne stands, choosing from paddocks where high plant populations had survived over many years. That approach starts from plants which have already proved they can persist, then selects among them for superior forage yield and improved disease and pest tolerance.

The result is a moderately tall plant with leafy stems and a high leaf to stem ratio, which is what determines feed quality in a lucerne. With a winter activity rating of six to seven it produces well through winter, spring and summer wherever moisture is available, and recovers vigorously after cutting or grazing.

Its practical strength is performing in sites where disease susceptible varieties will not persist. Lucerne stands are most often lost to root and crown disease rather than to grazing or drought, so disease tolerance is effectively stand life, and stand life is what determines whether the establishment cost is recovered.

details.tagline: High yielding quality hay
details.description:
L70 is a lucerne selected for hay production, and it is chosen where the crop is grown to be cut rather than grazed.

Hay lucerne is judged on quality as much as tonnage, and quality in lucerne is largely a question of leaf retention. Fine stems dry faster and more evenly than coarse ones, and leaf that stays attached through raking and baling is leaf that ends up in the bale rather than on the ground. L70 combines fine stems with good leaf retention for that reason.

Recovery after cutting is vigorous, which determines how many cuts a season will yield and therefore the return from the stand.

It suits both dryland and irrigated lucerne country, and like all lucernes it fixes nitrogen strongly, so the paddock is left in better condition for whatever follows.

L70 is a straightforward choice for growers whose primary objective is quality hay rather than a dual purpose grazing and cutting stand.

L91 is a lucerne selected for improved forage production, offering more consistent yield across the season rather than a single strong flush.

That consistency is what suits it to mixed use. A stand that produces reliably through the year can be cut when there is surplus and grazed when there is not, which gives a producer flexibility that a highly seasonal variety does not.

Recovery after cutting or grazing is strong, and good disease resistance underpins the stand life needed to recover the cost of establishing a lucerne paddock in the first place.

It suits hay, grazing and silage, and works in cropping rotations where the lucerne phase is expected to fix nitrogen and improve soil structure before the paddock returns to crop.

L91 is a dependable general purpose lucerne rather than a specialist one, appropriate where the paddock has to do several jobs across a few years.

details.description:
Chico is a chicory selected for high yield and very high feed quality, with fast establishment and rapid regrowth, and it is used principally as a specialist summer crop.

Chicory is a broad-leafed perennial herb with a thick, deep taproot, and that taproot is why it produces when grasses have stopped. It reaches moisture well below the root zone of a ryegrass, so growth continues through summer and autumn when the rest of the pasture has dried off. Chico is specifically noted for strong summer and autumn growth.

Feed quality is the other half of the case. Chicory is highly digestible with mineral levels above those of most grasses, and stock perform well on it, which is why it is used in high livestock performance systems for finishing young stock rather than as general pasture.

Chico carries strong insect resistance and good drought tolerance, and it establishes fast, forming basal rosettes of large, soft leaves before it runs up to flower.

It suits well drained, deeper soils and is best used where the summer feed gap is the constraint on the operation.

Ecotain is a plantain selected for an environmental function as well as an agronomic one. It is a highly effective nitrogen leaching mitigation technology, reducing the nitrogen lost from a grazing system to groundwater, which matters increasingly where catchment rules or water quality obligations apply.

It works as forage at the same time. Ecotain has erect growth and broad leaves, which maximises intake per bite and therefore drives animal performance, and it carries a coarse fibrous root system that is very efficient at extracting nutrients from the soil profile.

It offers winter activity together with drought tolerance, a combination that keeps it producing across a longer part of the year than most herbs, and it delivers animal health performance benefits across virtually all high performing pastoral systems, suiting beef, dairy and lamb enterprises.

Ecotain is adapted to many climates and soil types and will persist through hot summers and wet winters provided it is not overgrazed under those conditions, which is the main management consideration with the species.

details.tagline: Warm season grass for permanent pastures
details.description:
Bermuda grass is a warm season perennial that has consistently proved one of the best grasses for irrigated summer pastures in Australia, and it is increasingly used as a source of green forage and hay as well as for permanent pasture.

Its root system is the reason it persists. Bermuda roots extensively and deeply, which gives it the best chance of surviving tough drought conditions, and the structure of those roots also allows it to come through extended periods of waterlogging.

Above and below ground it spreads by runners: stolons across the surface and rhizomes beneath it. That makes the grass genuinely self-repairing, so bare patches remaining after the initial sowing are usually filled without a second sowing being needed, and it is why Bermuda holds a paddock so well under traffic and heavy grazing.

It performs best on moderately acid ground but tolerates more alkaline conditions, and it is suited to country where soluble salts in the water restrict what else can be grown. Good hay yields are achievable under irrigation with adequate fertiliser.

details.tagline: Dehulled Bermuda for fast establishing summer pasture
details.description:
Speedie is a Bermuda couch supplied dehulled, and the dehulling is the point of it. Bermuda seed carries a hull that slows water uptake and delays germination; removing it means the seed germinates a little quicker than normal unhulled Bermuda grass, which tightens up establishment and reduces the period when the seedling is exposed.

Bermuda grass itself has consistently proved one of the best perennial grasses for irrigated summer pastures in Australia, with a bright green, purple tipped blade. It has an extensive root system that survives both drought and extended waterlogging, and it spreads by stolons above ground and rhizomes below, which makes it excellent at self-repairing bare patches.

That combination of durability and self-repair is why it is used for green forage and hay, for permanent summer pasture, and as a turf grass on sports fields.

It suits irrigated country, and is a practical choice for smaller holdings running a few horses or cattle as well as for commercial pasture and hay production.

details.tagline: Performs well in acidic and low fertility soils
details.description:
Callide is a tetraploid Rhodes grass with a high number of growing points and a more prostrate growth habit than many alternatives, and it is one of the standard sub-tropical perennial grasses for summer rainfall country.

Growing points determine how a grass recovers. A plant carrying many of them can be grazed and come back from multiple sites rather than depending on a few, which is what allows Callide to handle grazing pressure and to thicken up over time.

It is summer active wherever soil moisture is available and adaptable to a wide range of soil types, which makes it broadly useful rather than district specific.

Two limitations shape where it belongs. Callide is less cold tolerant than other Rhodes varieties, so it suits warmer country and is generally sown north rather than south, and it is not tolerant of saline conditions, so saltland calls for a different species. Within those bounds it is a robust and productive perennial base.

details.description:
Carpet grass is a short, dense, mat-forming perennial that spreads by stolons, and it is chosen for country where better grasses will not grow.

Its case is tolerance rather than production. Carpet grass performs on poor soils of low fertility and it tolerates shade, which is unusual among pasture and turf grasses and makes it useful under trees and in situations where light is limited. It is an alternative to kikuyu and Bermuda couch where those species struggle.

It forms a dense mat that holds the ground, suppresses weeds and stands up to traffic, which is why it is used for ground cover as much as for feed.

Its limits are clear and worth stating: carpet grass is neither drought tolerant nor salt tolerant, so it needs reliable moisture and non-saline ground.

Finecut is a Rhodes grass bred from Katambora to improve on it in the traits that determine feed quality and hay value.

The differences are consistent. Finecut has finer leaves and stems than Katambora and a more upright growth habit, which lifts palatability and makes it considerably better suited to hay, since fine material cures faster and more evenly in the windrow. It also carries improved dry matter production and an increased leaf to stolon ratio, meaning more of the plant is feed rather than runner.

Flowering is uniform, which matters for hay timing: a crop that heads evenly can be cut at the right stage across the whole paddock rather than being part-mature and part-stemmy.

Over time Finecut has established itself across a wide range of soil types and farming systems through both northern and southern Western Australia, and it carries some tolerance of saline conditions.

It suits grazing, silage and hay, and is a mainstay of the sub-tropical perennial mixes.

details.tagline: Deep rooted and drought persistent
details.description:
Gatton panic is a deep rooted sub-tropical perennial grass, similar to green panic but with broader, darker green leaves, and more robust than either Bambatsi or Petrie.

Its root depth is what makes it drought persistent, and its root distribution is what makes it responsive. The root system is concentrated in the upper layers of the soil, which allows the plant to react quickly to light showers that a deeper rooted grass would not register, while still carrying enough depth to survive dry periods. It is summer active wherever soil moisture is available and is generally quick to respond after the first autumn rains.

Gatton is also efficient in how it stores reserves. More of its surplus carbohydrate accumulates in the upper part of the plant, where stock can eat it, rather than being locked below ground.

It withstands reasonable grazing pressure, and grows on soil types from heavy grey and brown clays through scrub loams to sands, though on lighter country it needs good nutrition to persist.

Katambora is a diploid Rhodes grass, earlier flowering than Callide and more cold tolerant, and that cold tolerance is what defines where it belongs: it can be sown south of Perth, where Callide struggles.

It has a very prostrate growth habit and a high number of growing points, which is what allows it to recover after grazing and to thicken into a dense sward over time rather than opening up.

It is summer active wherever soil moisture is available, and it is widely adapted across soil types.

Katambora is variable in its flowering and is coarser in leaf and stem than more recent releases, so it is less palatable than Finecut, Reclaimer or Callide. Where feed quality is the priority a newer variety will do better; where cold tolerance and reliability at lower cost are what matter, Katambora remains the practical choice, and it continues to appear in sub-tropical mixes for exactly that reason.

details.tagline: Robust perennial that handles cold and wet
details.description:
Narok is a setaria, a robust sub-tropical perennial with a vigorous growth habit, used in beef and dairy pasture and notable for withstanding temperatures below minus three degrees.

That cold tolerance is unusual in a sub-tropical grass and extends the country setaria can be grown on, into highland and cooler districts where most tropical species would be lost to frost.

It offers good regrowth after grazing and good tolerance of waterlogging, which suits it to heavier and wetter ground, with fair tolerance of heavy grazing, salinity and frost.

Setaria combines well with tropical legumes such as glycine and siratro, and a legume component is worth including, since it supplies nitrogen and lifts the protein content of the sward.

Two things are worth knowing. Setaria seed is very small, so sowing depth and seedbed preparation matter more than with a larger seeded grass. And the species may contain oxalate at certain growth stages, so it should not be the sole feed source for horses.

details.tagline: High salinity tolerance across a wide soil spectrum
details.description:
Reclaimer is an early maturing, erect, warm season Rhodes grass bred specifically for increased production in saline areas, and it retains the quality attributes of Finecut while adding salt tolerance.

Trials indicate that established Reclaimer will remain productive in saline conditions of between four and ten deciSiemens per metre, and could survive up to twenty. The qualifier matters: as an establishing plant it may struggle where it is sown into ground already affected by surface salt, so establishment needs to be timed for when winter rain has flushed salt down the profile.

It is highly stoloniferous with increased stolon density and more growing points than its predecessors, forming a dense mat over the ground more rapidly than other varieties. That creeping habit binds the soil and provides good erosion control, which is valuable on the scalded ground where saline pasture is usually being re-established.

Dry matter production is up to twenty per cent above Katambora, with early uniform flowering, and it carries the finer stems and increased palatability of Finecut, so it suits grazing, silage and hay.

details.tagline: Annual summer grass offering multiple harvests
details.description:
Teff is a fast establishing, summer active annual grass that has gained ground as a high quality forage crop producing good yields from low inputs, and it is one of the more flexible summer options available.

Its main strength is regrowth. Teff can be harvested multiple times through a season as hay, silage or grazing, so a single sowing produces several cuts rather than one, which changes the economics of a summer forage crop considerably.

The feed itself is fine stemmed, leafy and soft, highly palatable and nutritious, and once established the crop is fairly drought hardy.

Teff is also non-toxic, which is a genuine point of difference in summer forage. Sorghums and millets carry prussic acid or nitrate risks under stress that require management; teff does not, so it can be grazed by all livestock including horses without that concern.

It suits growers wanting cost effective summer feed with high dry matter potential, and it responds well to irrigation and to nitrogen, though it may lodge where both are pushed hard.

details.tagline: Deep rooted, self-repairing perennial grass
details.description:
Whittet is a taller growing variety of kikuyu, selected to produce more feed than the standard types while keeping the self-repairing habit that makes kikuyu so durable.

Kikuyu is a mat-forming perennial that spreads by underground stems and stolons, which is why it holds soil, tolerates trampling and recovers from heavy grazing. Whittet carries that with broader leaves, thicker stems and larger internodes on the stolons, all of which reflect its greater vigour, and it is a vigorous grower producing quick cover.

The trait that distinguishes it most usefully is persistence under lower fertility than other kikuyu varieties require. Kikuyu generally responds strongly to nitrogen and can decline where fertility is not maintained; Whittet holds on better in that situation.

Forage quality is high when the plant is managed correctly, which in practice means grazing it hard enough and often enough to keep it leafy, since kikuyu allowed to bulk up becomes stemmy and its quality falls away quickly.

details.tagline: Microbial biofertiliser for nitrogen, phosphorus and potash
details.description:
Bio NPK Powder S is a highly concentrated microbial biofertiliser, and it works on the three major nutrients by three different mechanisms.

Nitrogen it fixes from the atmosphere, converting it into forms the plant can take up. Phosphorus it solubilises: most soils hold considerably more phosphorus than plants can access, locked into compounds that roots cannot use, and the microbes release it. Potassium it mobilises from soil reserves in the same way.

Alongside the nutrient effect it enhances root systems and improves soil structure, and it strengthens plant resistance to abiotic stresses such as drought.

Microbial biostimulants of this type have been shown to improve both the physical and biological properties of soil, including root development, water holding capacity and general microbial activity, and increased microbial activity is what drives nutrient availability over the longer term.

It suits growers reducing reliance on synthetic fertiliser, or looking to get more out of the nutrient reserves a paddock already holds, and it promotes soil biodiversity as it works.

details.tagline: Liquid enzyme product for agricultural use
details.description:
BioSplito is a liquid enzyme product for agricultural use, supplied as a yellowish liquid and made up of an enzyme complex with surfactants in a water base.

It contains microorganisms selected from the natural environment which are not pathogenic to humans, animals or plants, and the mixture is biodegradable. It is not classified as dangerous under European classification regulations.

Handling is straightforward but the storage requirements matter, because the active component is biological. Keep it in tightly closed containers in a cool, dry, well ventilated place out of direct sunlight, ideally between five and thirty degrees.

Compatibility is the point to watch. BioSplito should be protected from strong acids, bases and oxidising agents, and from disinfectants, biocides and chemical pesticides, all of which will damage the biology the product depends on. It should not be tank mixed with these.

Standard precautions apply when handling: avoid inhaling spray mist, and wear protective goggles, gloves and workwear.

details.tagline: Peat inoculant for pasture and pulse legumes
details.description:
NoduleN Peat is a peat based rhizobial inoculant for pasture and pulse legumes, carrying highly productive Rhizobia strains at 1x10^9 CFU per gram at the time of manufacture.

Rhizobia are the soil bacteria that work with legumes to take atmospheric nitrogen from soil air spaces and fix it into nodules on the plant's roots. Inoculating with a selected strain significantly improves nodulation and plant performance even where background Rhizobia are already present in the soil, because the introduced strains are more effective than the naturalised population.

The numbers are worth understanding. A legume nodulated with the correct Rhizobium is estimated to fix between thirty and two hundred kilograms of nitrogen per hectare annually, equivalent to sixty-four to four hundred and thirty-two kilograms of urea, and the residual nitrate benefits the following crop's yield and protein.

The peat carrier holds moisture and nutrients that help the bacteria survive on the seed. NoduleN must contact the seed to work, and can be applied either as a slurry seed treatment or by liquid injection into the furrow. There is a nil withholding period.

products.descriptionSource: Rewritten from master catalogue tech sheets

details.blurb: A natural biofumigant grown in areas where soil borne pests and diseases are a problem. It also boosts overall productivity, suppresses weeds, and reaches maturity in approximately 12 to 14 weeks.

details.tagline: Natural biofumigant for pest and disease control
details.description:
Black mustard is grown as a biofumigant, a cover crop used to reduce soil borne pests and diseases through the chemistry of the plant itself rather than through an applied product.

Brassicas contain glucosinolates, and when the plant tissue is broken down these release isothiocyanates, compounds with genuine fumigant activity against soil pathogens and nematodes. Incorporating the crop into the soil while it is still green is what triggers the reaction, so timing and method of incorporation determine how much benefit is obtained.

Alongside that effect it works as a conventional cover crop, producing biomass quickly, suppressing weeds through competition and shading, and improving soil structure as the residue breaks down.

Black mustard suits intensive horticultural and high production cropping ground where soil borne disease has built up and rotation alone is not clearing it, and it is used either as a stand-alone break or as a component in a biofumigant blend alongside other brassicas.

details.tagline: Fast establishment with high feed value and yield
details.description:
Bounty is a forage sorghum selected for fast establishment and strong early vigour, producing high feed value and high dry matter yields through the warm months.

Establishment speed is what determines the value of a summer forage crop. The sowing window is bounded by soil temperature at one end and by the end of summer moisture at the other, so a crop that gets away quickly captures more of the season and reaches its first grazing sooner.

From there Bounty recovers quickly after grazing or cutting, which is what allows multiple harvests from a single sowing and is where the economics of forage sorghum are decided.

It suits direct grazing, hay and silage, and works as a cost effective way of producing summer bulk where the alternative is buying feed in.

As with all forage sorghums, soil temperature at sowing matters: sowing into cold soil gives slow germination and leaves seedlings exposed to disease and insect attack, so it is worth waiting for the soil to reach the mid teens and rising.

products.name: Buckwheat
products.descriptionSource: Rewritten from master catalogue tech sheets

details.blurb: Is not a cereal but a speedy short season summer cover crop option with a dense root system providing a good soil conditioner before the next autumn crop. Cover crops suppress weeds and attract beneficial insects and pollinators with their abundant blossoms. Good companion to add to a cover crop mix.
details.notes: NEW ROW (added from the 2026 guide). Not previously a catalogue product. NOTE: a 'Buckwheat' file already exists in the source library but was routed to Reference Notes because it is a generic University of Missouri Extension guide with no IH/AGF branding — this row is built from the 2026 guide instead, which does list Buckwheat as an IH Seeds line.
details.tagline: Summer cover crop option
details.description:
Buckwheat is not a cereal. It is a broadleaf plant whose seed is used much as a grain would be, which is why it is often called a pseudocereal, and in a farming system here it is grown for what it does to a paddock rather than for what comes off it.

Its defining trait is speed. Buckwheat sets seed faster than any other grain crop, which is why it has traditionally been grown where summers are short, and why it fits a window too tight for anything else.

In a cover cropping programme that speed does the work. A stand closes over fast and is regarded as one of the best options for smothering mid-summer weeds, not because individual plants compete hard, but because the canopy shuts out light early. Below ground a dense, fine root system opens up and conditions the topsoil ahead of the next autumn sowing.

Buckwheat also appears to be unusually good at making soil phosphorus available, releasing it as the residue breaks down. It responds poorly to superphosphate but well to rock phosphate.

The flowers are the other reason it earns a place, blossoming heavily over several weeks and drawing bees and beneficial insects in numbers. It is a warm season summer annual, most often used as one component of a multi-species cover crop mix.

details.tagline: Drought and heat tolerant summer forage legume
details.description:
Buff is a cowpea, an annual summer forage legume with a spreading growth habit, and it is one of the more useful legumes for the warm season.

Cowpeas tolerate both drought and heat, which is what suits them to summer country where a temperate legume would fail, and they can be used in several ways: fattening cattle and sheep, as a green manure to lift soil nitrogen, or cut for hay and silage, particularly in a mix with forage sorghum or millet where the legume lifts the protein of a grass-dominant crop.

That companion role is where cowpeas are most often used. A summer grass crop grown alone is bulky but low in protein; a cowpea component raises the quality of both the standing feed and the conserved product.

They grow on a variety of soils but will not tolerate waterlogging, so drainage matters more than fertility.

Seed should be inoculated with group I inoculant before sowing to ensure nodulation and nitrogen fixation, without which most of the benefit is lost.

details.tagline: Inexpensive, easy to establish winter green manure
details.description:
Cereal rye, also known as ryecorn, is a winter to spring cereal used principally as a green manure and cover crop, and its strength is that it is inexpensive and easy to establish.

Few other cool season green manure crops are as productive on genuinely poor soils. That is the case for it: on sandy, infertile country where a more demanding crop would not justify the sowing, cereal rye will still produce substantial biomass, and it can be used to build fertility on soils that need it.

Its extensive root system takes up excess nitrogen that would otherwise leach beyond the root zone over winter. That nitrogen is then released slowly as the residue decomposes, becoming available to the following cash crop, so the crop acts as a storehouse rather than a consumer.

The same root system opens up and conditions the soil profile.

Cereal rye suits growers wanting a low cost, reliable winter cover on light or degraded country, and it can be grazed before being incorporated where feed is also needed.

details.tagline: Fine leafed hybrid with excellent palatability
details.description:
Chomper is a fast growing, fine leafed hybrid sorghum with excellent palatability, and it is bred for systems where the crop will be harvested repeatedly rather than grazed out once.

The plant is a vigorous, erect grower with branched tillers reaching two to three metres, but its useful characteristic is the fine leaf and high leaf to stem ratio. Sorghums are often criticised for coarse stems that stock leave behind; a fine stemmed, leafy hybrid is eaten more completely and is far better suited to hay, where thick stems cure slowly and unevenly.

Seedling vigour is very good, and regrowth after cutting or grazing is quick, which is what makes multiple cuttings practical.

It can be intensively grazed once it has reached about a metre, with excellent recovery between grazings, and it produces very good hay and silage.

Chomper suits fertile heavier soils with good water holding capacity, and as with all sorghums it should not be sown until soil temperatures have reached the mid teens and are rising.

details.tagline: Multipurpose legume for forage or soil improvement
details.description:
Common vetch is an annual legume grown for forage, for hay, and as a soil improver, and it is one of the more flexible legumes in a mixed farming rotation.

Its value in the rotation is substantial. Vetch is particularly valued for the benefit it leaves for the cereal and oilseed crops that follow, which is generally greater than that from other pulses, because it fixes nitrogen strongly and leaves a residue that breaks down readily.

As forage it produces well through winter and can be cut for hay or silage, or grazed, or incorporated as a green manure depending on what the season and the enterprise require. That flexibility is useful in a year that does not go to plan, since the decision about how to use it can be made late.

It is a common component of cover crop mixes, where it supplies the nitrogen fixing function alongside cereals and brassicas.

Vetch should be inoculated before sowing to ensure effective nodulation.

details.tagline: Excellent nitrogen fixation with multiple end uses
details.description:
Coogee is a field pea grown for both grain and forage, and it offers several routes to a return from one sowing.

Its main contribution in a rotation is nitrogen. Field peas fix nitrogen efficiently, leaving the soil in better condition for the cereal that follows and reducing the fertiliser nitrogen that crop requires, and as a broadleaf they also break cereal disease cycles.

The multiple end use options are what make the crop practical. Coogee can be taken through to grain, cut for hay or silage, grazed, or incorporated as green manure, and that decision can be made well into the season depending on prices, rainfall and feed requirements.

It fits stubble retention systems, where the standing stubble supports the crop and reduces the lodging that makes field peas difficult to harvest.

Peas are best sown into a well prepared seedbed at the right depth, and inoculation is required for effective nodulation.

details.description:
Ebony is an annual diploid summer legume with a spreading growth habit, released in Australia as a grazing type of cowpea for subtropical coastal areas with medium rainfall or under irrigation.

Its distinguishing feature is disease resistance. Ebony carries resistance to stem rot disease races three and four of Phytophthora vignae, the severe root rot fungus, and good tolerance of Phytophthora root disease generally. In country where that fungus is present, a susceptible cowpea will not persist, so the resistance is what makes the crop viable rather than merely better.

It offers a long production season and good drought tolerance, and it has no prussic acid issues, which distinguishes it from the sorghums that would otherwise occupy the same slot in a summer programme.

As a legume it is an excellent source of nitrogen in summer rotations and a good companion with millet and forage sorghum, lifting the protein content of the conserved feed. It also makes an excellent green manure crop.

The seed is large at around five thousand per kilogram, and requires group I inoculant. Ebony is susceptible to frost.

details.tagline: Dual purpose triticale for grazing and grain
details.description:
Endeavour is a long season, semi awnless dual purpose triticale, grown for both grazing and grain from the same sowing.

The dual purpose system is what it is built for. Being mid to late maturing, Endeavour can be sown very early, grazed through winter when feed is short and expensive, then shut up for either forage conservation or grain recovery. The grazing takes place before the growing point has elevated, so the crop recovers and still yields.

It has excellent grain and dry matter recovery after grazing, with grain yields commonly exceeding those of other varieties by ten to twenty per cent, which is what makes the grazing effectively free rather than a cost against the grain crop.

The semi awnless characteristic matters for grazing. Awns make a crop unpleasant for stock to eat and can cause mouth irritation, so a semi awnless type is grazed more willingly and more completely.

Endeavour can be sown as early as mid February where seasonal conditions allow, though March to early April is the more usual window.

details.blurb: A winter growing pulse crop, planted in mid to late autumn and harvested in late spring or early summer. Faba beans fit well in rotation with winter and summer cereals or cotton, making those rotations more productive and profitable. Nitrogen fixed in the root system becomes available to the next crop, reducing the need for fertiliser nitrogen, and levels of soil-borne diseases such as crown rot and root lesion nematode are reduced by growing faba bean as a break crop.
details.notes: ⚠ The source document itself has unfilled placeholder values for pH, rainfall, sowing rate, and days-to-flowering (the text literally reads 'CaCl2 +', 'xx to xxmm+', 'xxkg/ha', 'xx') — these key figures were apparently never completed by IH Seeds and could not be extracted. Only one source file was found for this product (no duplicate or updated version to cross-check) — Douglas should obtain the missing agronomic figures to complete this record.
details.tagline: Winter pulse that lifts nitrogen for the next crop
details.description:
Faba bean is a cool season pulse grown across southern Australia as both a food legume and a rotation tool. It is sown in mid to late autumn and harvested in late spring or early summer, developing quickly through July to September as it flowers and sets pod. Flowering stops as daytime temperatures approach thirty degrees, which is what sets the northern limit of where the crop is worth growing.

The plant reaches about a metre and a half, erect, throwing stems from its base over a taproot that carries a mass of fibrous roots through the top thirty centimetres of soil. Flowering begins low on the stem in early varieties and progressively higher in later ones, then continues up the plant over six to ten weeks. Like most legumes it sets far more flowers than it can carry, and fewer than fifteen per cent go on to make pods. Honeybees working the flowers cross-pollinate at rates commonly between twenty-five and thirty per cent.

Where faba beans earn their place is the rotation. Sequences that put a faba bean phase between winter and summer cereals, or ahead of cotton, are consistently more productive and more profitable than those without a legume, because yield and quality lift in the crop that follows. Up to forty per cent of the crop's nitrogen sits below ground, cutting the fertiliser nitrogen the next crop needs and adding to soil organic nitrogen. Growers also report better soil tilth afterwards.

details.tagline: Early flowering hybrid for earlier grazing
details.description:
FeedEx is an early to mid-season flowering hybrid sorghum, flowering at around eighty-two days, and that earliness is the reason to choose it: it provides grazing opportunities sooner than later flowering varieties, which matters when a summer feed gap has to be filled quickly.

It is high yielding with quick recovery after grazing or cutting, so the crop can be harvested repeatedly through the season, and it suits direct grazing, silage or hay.

Its stems are finer than many forage sorghums, which improves both intake and curing for hay, and its cold tolerance is excellent for the type, giving a little more latitude at either end of the sowing window. Disease-wise it carries intermediate resistance to most races of rust and leaf blight.

FeedEx is best suited to country with good underlying soil moisture or irrigation through the growing period, since sorghum will not finish what it starts without moisture behind it.

It is also a lower cost option for producing late spring and summer forage in place of bought-in feed, and works as a cover or green manure crop.

details.description:
Freyrs is a sunn hemp, a tropical legume grown as a summer cover crop, and it is best suited to the warmer districts north of Perth.

Its value is a combination of speed and nitrogen. Sunn hemp grows very quickly in warm conditions, producing substantial biomass in a short window, and as a legume it fixes nitrogen while it does so, which means the cover crop is building fertility rather than simply occupying the ground.

It also suppresses nematodes, which makes it useful ahead of crops sensitive to nematode pressure and adds a disease break function to the biomass and nitrogen benefits.

The biomass is coarse, and the crop is generally grown to be incorporated or left as surface residue rather than grazed hard, though it can be used as forage.

Freyrs suits growers wanting a warm season legume cover in northern districts, where its heat requirement is met and where the summer window is long enough for it to produce properly.

details.tagline: Highly palatable rape with strong regrowth
details.description:
Hobson is a forage brassica with good palatability and strong regrowth, and it is grown to fill the summer feed gap when pasture production has been cut short by heat and lack of rain.

Its long taproot is what allows it to do that. Where a shallow rooted crop runs out of water as the topsoil dries, Hobson chases moisture down the profile and keeps producing into the dry period.

Palatability is where it stands out. It is the preferred brassica for grazing on account of exceptional palatability, and a brassica stock take to readily is used far more completely than one they eat reluctantly, which changes the return from the paddock.

It is fast to first grazing at ten to twelve weeks and offers good regrowth afterwards, so more than one grazing is normally available.

Hobson can be sown in autumn or spring depending on when the feed is required, and it is a useful component in biofumigant blends thanks to its suppression of nematodes.

details.tagline: Fast growing summer crop for quick feed
details.description:
Japanese millet is a quick maturing summer forage crop, sown mainly in late spring once soil temperatures are high and there has been good summer rainfall.

Its value is entirely in speed. Japanese millet can grow to a metre in forty-five days and can be grazed within about six weeks of emergence depending on rainfall, which makes it the crop to reach for when feed is needed quickly through the hot dry months from January to March.

That speed also makes it an effective weed suppressing cover crop, and its fibrous root system is good for controlling erosion on ground that would otherwise be left bare.

It is often described as a last resort late in the season, and that is a fair characterisation of how it is commonly used: when other options have passed their sowing window, millet will still produce something.

It is best suited to lighter soils than a forage sorghum requires, and it carries no prussic acid risk, which simplifies grazing management considerably.

details.tagline: Versatile, reliable and high yielding
details.description:
Joey is a triticale, a hybrid of wheat and rye, and the hybrid explains what the crop offers. It combines the hardiness of rye with the productivity of wheat, giving high yields and quality feed on country where wheat alone would struggle.

It is known for excellent winter forage and fast growth, with good tolerance of both drought and acid soils. Acid tolerance in particular widens the country it can be grown on, since soil acidity limits root growth and therefore yield for many cereals.

Joey is versatile across end uses: grazing, hay, silage and cover cropping are all practical from the same sowing, and that flexibility is worth a good deal in a season that does not develop as expected.

It suits growers wanting reliable winter feed with the option of taking the crop through to grain or conserving it, particularly on lighter or more acid country where wheat is marginal.

details.description:
Karaka is an annual hybrid brassica, a leafy turnip type, and it is grown for fast, high quality feed from a short sowing-to-grazing window.

Its defining characteristic is how quickly it is ready and how often it can be grazed. Karaka delivers quick, palatable feed and produces high yields through multiple grazings when grown on fertile soils and managed effectively, so it is not a single-harvest crop.

The feed itself is highly palatable and of high quality, which makes it particularly suitable for finishing stock and for lifting condition quickly.

Fertility is the main determinant of performance. Karaka responds strongly to good soil nutrition and will not produce to its potential on poor country, so it is best placed on the better paddocks or supported with fertiliser.

It suits summer and autumn feed gaps, sown either alone or with a companion such as a leafy annual grass, and grazing management is what determines how many grazings are actually achieved.

details.tagline: Semi-dwarf pearl millet with no prussic acid
details.description:
Lawrence is a semi-dwarf pearl millet, and it exists because until relatively recently there were no pearl millet varieties that could be grown under the cool temperate conditions of southern Australia. Pearl millet is a semi-arid tropical grass grown for grain and forage across the tropical world, and Lawrence brought it into a colder growing environment.

It produces high yields of forage over a relatively short growing season, growing rapidly and ready to cut or graze six to eight weeks after planting, at around a metre in height.

Its most practically important feature is that it does not produce prussic acid. Forage sorghums require careful grazing management because prussic acid accumulates under stress and after frost, presenting a real poisoning risk; pearl millet removes that constraint entirely, which simplifies management and reduces risk with young or valuable stock.

Dry matter yield is similar to forage sorghum, so the safety comes without a yield penalty. It suits fresh fodder, silage or hay.

details.blurb: A mustard variety used as a biofumigant in high production agricultural areas where soil borne pests and diseases are a problem. details.tagline: Mustard biofumigant for soil borne pests
details.description:
Nemnuke is a mustard variety used as a biofumigant, grown in high production agricultural areas where soil borne pests and diseases have built up.

It works through the plant's own chemistry. Nemnuke contains glucosinolates, natural compounds which release isothiocyanates, a powerful fumigant known for delaying the onset and reducing the severity of root rot and bacterial wilt. Incorporating the crop while green is what releases the compounds, so how and when the crop is worked in determines the result.

Beyond the fumigant effect it functions as a substantial cover crop. It increases soil organic carbon levels, improves soil structure, and lifts the soil's nutrient and moisture holding capacity, all of which improve productivity beyond the immediate disease benefit. It also suppresses weeds through competition and canopy cover.

Nemnuke suits horticultural and intensive cropping ground where rotation alone is not clearing disease pressure, and it reaches maturity in approximately twelve to fourteen weeks.

details.blurb: An annual pasture legume for winter-wet saltland areas with more than 375mm annual rainfall, Neptune has a higher combined tolerance of salinity and waterlogging than all other current pasture legumes. It was the most productive and persistent of 21 varieties trialled over three years on saline, waterlogged soils in WA and South Australia. It can be safely grazed and will supply nitrogen to soils that are generally highly nitrogen deficient, provided it is inoculated with the salt-tolerant messina Rhizobium.

details.tagline: The most salt and waterlogging tolerant legume
details.description:
Neptune is a messina, an aerial-seeding annual legume growing up to eighty centimetres tall, native to the Mediterranean basin and identified as the only pasture legume able to persist on severely saline, waterlogged soils. That identification came from work by the Department of Primary Industries and Regional Development and SARDI as part of the Future Farm Industries CRC, and Neptune was subsequently selected as the most productive and persistent variety of the species.

It has higher combined tolerance of salinity and waterlogging than any other current pasture legume. In trials across five sites in Western Australia and South Australia over three years it was the most productive and persistent of twenty-one varieties, out-producing the three best existing options for saline land by a wide margin.

Its germination behaviour is central to that performance. Neptune germinates at salinity levels that stop other legumes, which matters because topsoil salinity peaks over summer and autumn when germinating rains arrive. Delayed seed softening defers germination until rainfall is more likely to have flushed salt from the surface.

Green plants have high nutritive value with high digestibility and crude protein and no known toxic chemicals. Neptune is recommended for use in mixed pastures rather than alone, since a saline paddock varies and different species occupy different niches within it.
