details.tagline: Traditional dun field pea for stubble retention
details.description:
Parafield is a traditional Australian dun field pea, purple flowering with dimpled beige to brown seed, mid-season maturing with increased pod set and vigour.

It fits stubble retention systems with no tillage particularly well, using the standing stubble as a supportive trellis. That is more useful than it sounds: field peas are prone to lodging, and a crop held up by stubble is easier to harvest and less exposed to disease at ground level. Sowing depth matters, and stubble clumping should be avoided.

It has wide adaption from sandy loam through to heavy clays, and provides nitrogen fixation that benefits the following crop.

Parafield consistently outyields Alma, Dundale and the early dun peas, though its yield potential is below that of more recent releases, so it is chosen for reliability and adaptation rather than maximum yield.

Its main limitation is lodging. Although tall, conventional-leaved plants are almost always prostrate at maturity and must be picked up close to the soil surface at harvest. The seed is used for both animal and human consumption, including forage and hay.

details.tagline: Tall black seeded grazing oat with fine stems
details.description:
Saia is a tall, black seeded grazing oat with a fine stem, grown as a fast-establishing autumn to spring fodder crop.

Its fine stem and high leaf to stem ratio are what set it apart from a standard grazing oat. Fine stemmed material is eaten more completely, cures faster for hay, and holds its quality better than a coarse crop, so the feed value of what is grown is higher even where the tonnage is similar.

It establishes quickly and provides good quality feed for hay and silage as well as grazing, and pastures rebound well after grazing, so more than one grazing is normally available.

It is a tufted annual growing to nearly two metres, late maturing, and it grows across a wide range of soil types with good tolerance of acid soils, which widens the country it suits.

Saia is used in cover crop situations as well as for forage, and is readily palatable to sheep, cattle and horses.

details.description:
Shirohie is the most commonly available temperate millet, with improved vigour and better recovery from grazing than the older Japanese variety it succeeded. The term Jap millet has been used loosely to describe temperate millets generally, which incorrectly implies there is little difference between the two.

The main advantage of the temperate millets is that they can be sown early, once soil temperatures reach around fourteen degrees and rising, which is well before a forage sorghum can go in. That produces earlier feed than the alternatives, filling a gap in the programme rather than competing with it.

High quality feed is produced, though total yield over the season is much lower than forage sorghum will deliver, so the two are complementary rather than interchangeable.

Shirohie can be sown on lighter soils than forage sorghum tolerates, but it needs supporting nutrition and good grazing management to reach its potential, and starter fertiliser is important for production through to the first grazing.

There is no hydrocyanic acid poisoning risk with temperate millets, which simplifies management considerably.

details.description:
Siberian is a temperate millet, a quick summer crop that is ideal for double cropping where a short window has to be used productively.

Its advantage over Shirohie is behavioural. Siberian has less tendency to run to head when under stress or in high summer temperatures, and running to head is what destroys the quality of a millet crop, since a plant that has gone reproductive puts its energy into seed rather than leaf and its feed value falls away quickly. A variety that stays vegetative longer under stress holds quality through the hottest part of the season.

Like other temperate millets it can be sown early, once soil temperatures reach around fourteen degrees and rising, producing feed ahead of alternatives such as sorghum. High quality feed is produced, though total seasonal yield is lower than a forage sorghum.

Siberian grows on all soil types including lighter country, and suits sheep and cattle for grazing and silage. It carries no prussic acid risk.

details.tagline: Good cover crop option to include in mixes
details.description:
Sunflower is grown here principally as a summer cover crop, valued for what it does to soil structure and for the insects it brings in rather than for a harvested product.

Its deep taproot is the primary reason to include it. The root loosens and conditions heavy soils, opening channels that persist after the crop has gone, and it improves structure, aeration and nutrient status as the residue breaks down. A broad-leaf canopy with dense growth suppresses weeds by shading them out.

The flowers attract bees and beneficial insects through the flowering phase, which is why sunflower is a common component of multi-species cover crop blends aimed at building on-farm biodiversity as well as soil.

Where it is grown for the cover crop effect rather than for seed, it is best slashed before flowering so the biomass goes back to the soil rather than into seed production.

It suits deep soils with good water holding capacity, and its taproot can extract water well below the reach of most crops.

details.description:
SuperSun 66 is a medium to late maturing sunflower, and its maturity is what allows it to maximise yield across a wide range of conditions rather than being tied to one season shape.

It reaches fifty per cent flower in approximately seventy-five days, with harvest at around one hundred and forty days depending on conditions. Standability is excellent and the seeds are large and plump, both of which matter at harvest: a crop that stands is harvested cleanly, and large seed improves both grade and handling.

SuperSun 66 suits no-till systems on deeper country, and the same deep rooting that drives its yield leaves the soil profile in better condition for the crop that follows.

details.tagline: Compaction buster with good forage production
details.description:
Buster is a tillage radish, grown to break up soil compaction biologically rather than mechanically.

Its large taproot drives down through compacted layers, and when the plant dies off the root decays and leaves a channel behind it. Those channels improve water infiltration and give the following crop's roots a path through a layer they could not otherwise penetrate, which is why the crop is described as a compaction buster. On many soils this is a cheaper and more durable answer than deep ripping.

The same deep root scavenges nutrients from below the root zone of shallower crops and brings them back to the surface as the residue breaks down, so nitrogen and other nutrients that would have leached are recovered.

Alongside the soil work it produces useful forage and grows fast enough to suppress weeds through canopy cover.

Buster suits compacted cropping ground, and is often sown in a multi-species cover crop blend where its rooting depth complements shallower rooted companions.

details.description:
White French millet originates from Eastern Europe and occupies a specific niche: it copes with hot, dry conditions better than other millets, which makes it the choice when the season has already turned difficult.

It tillers well with reasonable drought tolerance, and its maturity is short to medium depending on when it is sown. It will germinate once soil temperatures are above twelve degrees, which makes it an option for late winter or early spring sowing where winter crops have failed and the paddock needs something in it.

January and February are often the preferred planting times, since it provides useful growth when conditions are at their hottest.

It suits lighter sandy to clay loam soil types.

One limitation should be understood before sowing: the crop has a very open, drooping head and hairy leaves, and it is not suitable for grazing or hay. White French millet is therefore grown for seed and for cover rather than as a forage crop, which distinguishes it from Shirohie and Siberian.

details.description:
Winfred is a forage brassica, a cross between turnip and kale, and it is the all-rounder of the brassica range, suited to a wide spread of soil types, stock classes and sowing times.

That flexibility is the case for it. Where a specialist brassica has to be matched to a situation, Winfred performs across most of them, which makes planning simpler and reduces the risk of a mismatch.

It carries exceptional drought tolerance and good frost tolerance, so it holds on through conditions at both extremes, and it has excellent regrowth potential, giving the potential for two to four grazings between early summer and late winter rather than a single harvest.

Its flexibility extends the season too: it performs well through summer and can be carried later into the year as winter feed is required.

Winfred is a good companion species, sown with an Italian ryegrass to provide quick feed after sowing, or with herbs and clovers. Stock should be introduced to any brassica crop gradually, with the diet supplemented from another feed source.

The species are chosen for different functions. Some provide high levels of biomass for ground cover and organic matter; nitrogen fixing legumes build fertility; soil improvers work on structure and health; and others attract beneficial insects that support pest control across the wider farm.

Thirteen species is a deliberate choice rather than a marketing number. Diversity is what makes a cover crop resilient and effective, because different plants root at different depths, feed different soil organisms and respond differently to whatever the season does. Creating that biodiversity delivers benefits well beyond the individual paddock.

Cover crops protect ground that would otherwise sit bare for a large part of the year, which is where soil is lost and structure degrades.

The mix suits a wide range of soil types and conditions, and can be grazed, mulched or incorporated depending on the objective.

components.description: Prairie grass or Pasture Brome grass (Bromus sp.) is a grass that is tolerant to drier conditions due to deep root system. Its sugar and starch concentrations average around 10 to 15% in comparison to ryegrass at 30%+ and is highly palatable to the horse. Protein levels, as high as 12% are achieved at certain stages of its growth. This species of prairie/brome grass is specifically bred as a pasture grass and has no adverse effects on livestock, including horses.

Serradella is a winter dominant, deep rooted annual legume which grows mainly during the Autumn, Winter, and Spring months. Being a legume, it has good levels of protein, consistently low in sugars and starch, highly palatable to the horse, and provides nitrogen fixation to improve the soil quality.

Tall Fescue is another common horse pasture with reasonable (around 15%) sugar and starch levels, highly palatable for horses and provides an excellent swarth of feed when required. Growing reasonably well in drier conditions, its deep root system does give it some resistance to the dry. Its main growing period is late spring/early summer.

Teff grass is naturally low in sugars through most of the growing season plus fair protein levels (around 9%). During the plant’s young, growing stage, it is very palatable feed. As it matures though and starts to dry off, both its palatability and nutrient value start to fall. While it is a very good horse feed it does, like most C4 tropical grasses, contain an amount of oxalate (the calcium binding compound). While the oxalate concentration isn’t large, it is still present and therefore it is important that the Teff grass is not the only pasture species in the grazing paddock.

Finecut Rhodes grass is very resilient to drought and heavy traffic. Rhodes does most of its growing during later Spring/Summer before drying off. Rhodes grass retains very low concentrations of sugars in the leaves at most stages of growth. Coupled with good palatability and very low concentrations of oxalates, this makes Rhodes the ideal horse safe pasture species.

Callide Rhodes Grass being a tetraploid, Callide Rhodes grass is more palatable and tends to be preferentially grazed when sown with other sub-tropical grasses. Callide Rhodes grass has a high number of growing points with a more prostate growth habit than more recent releases and is coarser in the leaf and stem. It is also summer active where soil moisture is available.

Cocksfoot is a perennial tufted grass that is best grazed before flowering, and no lower than 5cm to allow for regrowth. Cocksfoot is hardy, drought resistant with deep roots. Endophyte free, tolerant to pest attack but can suffer from rust until established. Yarck Cocksfoot is a summer activity variety.

Lucerne provides a beneficial perennial legume component to this mix. Lucerne is a very nutritious feed and source of fibre. It contains about 18% high-quality protein which provides good levels of all the essential amino acids for horses, including lysine, which can be low in many feeds, including grains. It is high in digestible fibre, including pectin, which provides sustained energy (it is converted to glucose, glycogen, and fat in horses’ livers) and is very good for digestive health because it promotes beneficial gut microflora. Lucerne is readily available, very palatable, and highly digestible.

details.description:
Equi1st is an Irwin Hunter blend formulated specifically for horses, and it exists because horses are not cattle and should not be grazed as though they were.

Horses are not physiologically designed to cope with the high sugar and protein levels that traditional pasture mixes deliver. An ideal horse pasture is relatively low in sugars and starch and moderate in protein, while remaining palatable enough that the animal will eat it. That is a harder specification than it sounds, and it is why a general purpose pasture mix is a poor choice for a horse paddock.

Equi1st combines teff, prairie grass, serradella, tall fescue, Rhodes grasses, cocksfoot and lucerne, species selected for that sugar and protein profile rather than for maximum production. The blend is also tolerant of animal traffic and grazing, which matters on horse paddocks that carry concentrated use.

It improves the soil as it establishes, and it is suitable for all other livestock as well.

Because several components are tropical grasses that contain oxalate, the mix is designed so that no single species dominates the paddock.

details.description:
The Green Manure Mix is an Irwin Hunter blend of oats, faba beans and vetch, grown specifically to be returned to the soil rather than harvested.

Each component contributes something different. The oats produce bulk quickly and out-compete germinating weeds, and their fibrous roots break up the soil. The faba beans fix nitrogen and break the life cycle of cereal root diseases such as take-all and crown rot, and their shallow root system and shorter season mean soil moisture at depth is not fully drawn down. The vetch adds further nitrogen, and its benefit to the cereal and oilseed crops that follow is generally greater than that from other pulses.

Green manure improves soil that has been depleted by previous crops, or prepares ground for a crop that will be nutrient hungry. It also improves structure and water retention, and draws minerals up through the profile where following plants can reach them.

The crop is grown for roughly six weeks before mulching, and it can be grazed first to provide extra feed before it goes back into the ground.

details.description:
The IH Dairy Select Mix is an Irwin Hunter blend formulated specifically for the dairy industry, where the requirement is not simply tonnage but consistent, high quality feed delivered across the year.

Dairy pasture is judged differently from grazing pasture. Milk production responds to feed quality and to intake, so a blend for dairy has to combine varieties that stock will eat readily with a spread of maturities that avoids gaps in the feed curve, and it has to stand up to the high stocking rates a dairy platform carries.

The mix brings together proven ryegrasses with clovers to do exactly that, supporting high production of quality feed while the clover component contributes nitrogen to the grass and protein to the diet.

Sixty years of supplying Western Australian dairy farmers is what informs the formulation, and the blend is reviewed as varieties improve rather than being left to stand.

It suits irrigated and higher rainfall dairy country, and responds strongly to the nutrition a dairy platform normally receives.

details.description:
The Interow Mix is an Irwin Hunter blend for the ground between rows: vineyards, orchards, and any cropping situation where a cover is needed in the inter-row space.

The requirements there are different from a grazing paddock. The cover has to establish reliably, hold the soil against erosion and traffic, improve structure over time, and then stay low maintenance without competing unduly with the crop it sits beside.

Erosion control is often the immediate reason for sowing. Bare inter-row ground loses soil in heavy rain and compacts under machinery traffic, and a living cover addresses both, while its root system opens the profile and improves water infiltration.

The mix is chosen to tolerate the traffic that inter-row ground receives, and to persist without needing regular attention.

It also works as a general cover crop where a durable, low input ground cover is wanted, and it can be mown or left standing depending on the situation.

details.description:
The Irrigation Mix is an Irwin Hunter formulation for country where water is not the limiting factor, and where the objective is to convert that water into as much high quality feed as possible.

It combines ryegrasses with white clover. Under irrigation a ryegrass will produce heavily provided nutrition keeps up, and the white clover component supplies nitrogen to the grass while adding protein and palatability to the sward, which is why the two are almost always sown together in an irrigated pasture.

Irrigated pasture is an expensive asset, and getting the blend right matters more there than almost anywhere else. Sixty years of supplying irrigators across the state sits behind how this mix is put together.

It can be established from March onwards under an early watering programme, which brings the pasture into production sooner than a rainfall-dependent sowing would allow.

The mix produces strongly across the season and suits both grazing and fodder conservation, particularly in dairy systems where consistent quality feed through the year is the requirement.

details.description:
Nitro Mix is an Irwin Hunter blend built on a simple proposition: grow more, input less, and regenerate the soil while doing it.

The mix relies on biological nitrogen fixation rather than bought-in nitrogen. Legumes in association with the right rhizobia take nitrogen from the air and fix it into the soil, and a blend weighted towards that function reduces the synthetic fertiliser a paddock needs while building fertility rather than drawing it down.

Reducing reliance on synthetic nitrogen matters on two fronts. It is a direct saving on a significant input cost, and it moves the system towards one where soil biology and structure improve season on season instead of degrading.

Alongside the nitrogen, the mix improves soil structure and biological activity, which lifts water holding capacity and nutrient availability over time.

Nitro Mix suits growers moving towards a regenerative approach, or anyone looking to cut fertiliser costs without giving up production, and it can be grazed or worked in depending on the objective.

details.description:
The Tropical 80/20 Rule Mix is an Irwin Hunter blend of eighty per cent Gatton Panic with twenty per cent Reclaimer Rhodes Grass, pairing the most popular tropical pasture grass with the next most popular.

The ratio is the formulation. Gatton Panic provides the bulk of the pasture: deep rooted, drought persistent, withstanding reasonable grazing pressure, summer active wherever soil moisture is available, and quick to respond after the first autumn rains. Reclaimer, at the smaller proportion, brings what Gatton does not. It is strongly stoloniferous, binding the soil for erosion control and forming a dense mat over the ground, and it was bred for increased production in saline areas, so it holds the parts of a paddock where salt would otherwise limit growth.

Blending them means the pasture covers more of the variation within a paddock than either species could alone, which is the whole argument for a mix over a monoculture on variable country.

Sheep, cattle and horses all do well on it. As with any perennial tropical pasture, the stand should be left ungrazed until the plants are properly anchored.

details.grazingManagementNotes: Shut gate until well established (8-10 months); rotational grazing; graze in at 25-30cm down to residue of 12-15cm; do not overgraze over summer. Reclaimer Rhodes can be sown where grazing, silage and hay are required. After the first grazing has been completed move to a rotational grazing system where possible. Perennial pastures need a longer spell between grazing than temperate pastures to grow the herbage (biomass) to achieve the best production outcome.

components.description: Finecut Rhodes Grass has been bred from Katambora and offers improved dry matter production, increased leaf to stolon ratio over Katambora, has increased palatability and has excellent hay attributes. Finecut Rhodes has finer leaves and stems than Katambora, has a more upright growth habit and over time has established itself across a wide range of soil types and farming systems throughout northern and southern Western Australia. Finecut Rhodes can be sown where grazing, silage and hay are required.

Gatton Panic Grass is a medium height bunch grass variety of guinea grass similar to Green Panic. Gatton Panic has broader dark green leaves and smooth stem nodes, is highly adaptable and resilient, with the ability to establish across a wide rainfall zone. Gatton Panic will establish more easily than other panic grasses and can give very good first year production. Gatton Panic can be grown on lighter soil types but requires good soil nutrition to persist. Where practical remove weed burden before sowing. Sow on a well-prepared seedbed when soil temperatures are 16 – 18° C and rising. Sow no deeper than 2cm. It is recommended to shut the gate and only graze after 8 to 10 months or when plants are well anchored. If desired broadcast / sow any additional legumes in the first autumn after grazing, then re-introduce livestock to get seed to soil contact. Implement a rotational grazing system. Graze at 25 to 30cm and leave a residue of 12 to 15cm. Do not overgraze over summer. After the first grazing has been completed move to a rotational grazing system where possible. Perennial pastures need a longer spell between grazing than temperate pastures to grow the herbage (biomass) to achieve the best production outcome. Like temperate grasses, perennial / sub-tropical grasses will increase the below ground root mass as the above ground leaf mass accumulates, increasing the accumulation of water-soluble carbohydrates, (energy plants use) for later use to grow more biomass. By adopting a rotational grazing system using the height suggestions below as a guide, the retention of biomass after grazing and the subsequent root mass retained will act as a reserve to kick start the next period of leaf growth. It is important to reduce grazing pressure over summer, (unless there is adequate moisture for plant growth), or when seed set is occurring to provide the potential for some plant recruitment through seed set. Sow when soil temperatures are 16- 18° C and rising. Sow no deeper than 2cm. Katambora Rhodes Grass is a widely adapted, warm-season perennial valued for its persistence, drought tolerance and reliable forage production. It establishes quickly, forming a dense, leafy pasture with vigorous stolons that provide excellent ground cover, soil stabilisation and rapid recovery after grazing. Well suited to grazing, hay production and permanent pasture systems, Katambora performs across a wide range of well-drained soils under both dryland and irrigated conditions. It offers moderate salinity tolerance, produces high spring and summer dry matter yields and contributes to improved soil structure and reduced erosion.

details.description:
The WA Northern Perennial Pasture Mix is exclusive to Irwin Hunter Seeds. It is not a blend that can be bought elsewhere, and it exists because sixty years of trading into the northern districts has taught us which sub-tropical perennials actually hold on up there and in what proportions they work together.

The mix is built around Rhodes grass with Gatton Panic. Rhodes is highly stoloniferous, binding the soil and forming a dense mat that provides genuine erosion control on light country, while Gatton Panic brings depth of root, drought persistence and the ability to respond quickly to light showers that a deeper rooted grass would not register. The two occupy different parts of the profile and different parts of the season, which is why the combination outperforms either sown alone.

The formulation has not stood still. Its components have been reviewed and changed across editions as better varieties have become available, and the current blend reflects what is performing now rather than what performed a decade ago.

It suits northern grazing country where a perennial base is wanted for summer production, ground cover and stability, and it is best established with the paddock shut up until the plants are properly anchored.

Kikuyu (Pennisetum clandestinum) is a mat-forming perennial grass that spreads by underground stems. With a root system of up to 30 – 40cm on regularly grazed pasture, Kikuyu is tolerant of trampling, holds the soils and responds to high manure input. It is moderately drought tolerant and is highly productive during periods of high humidity. Kikuyu can tolerate some waterlogging and moderate salinity levels. It can tolerate soil pH as low as 4.5. Grows best in temperatures between 15 – 25°C but will tolerate up to 40°C. Kikuyu is very effective for erosion control, suppresses weeds, survives long dry periods, is highly persistent and responds well to nitrogen fertiliser in a warm season.

A great all-rounder with high winter forage yields and some summer production under favourable conditions. Amplify has the ability to go summer dormant under adverse conditions for increased persistence. A long term perennial pasture that gives you increased seedling vigour and lower toxicity. Amplify is a smart choice for growers who want a reliable and high yielding long term pasture. details.description:
The WA Southern Perennial Pasture Mix is an Irwin Hunter blend bringing together panic and Rhodes grasses with phalaris and kikuyu, formulated as a perennial base for southern Western Australian country.

Combining sub-tropical and temperate perennials in one mix is deliberate. The sub-tropical grasses produce through summer where moisture allows and hold the ground through heat; phalaris is a deep rooted temperate perennial that tolerates waterlogging and salinity and produces through winter and spring. Together they cover a far wider part of the year than either group alone, which is the point of a perennial pasture in the first place.

Kikuyu contributes ground cover and resilience, spreading by underground stems and stolons, tolerating trampling, holding soil and responding to manure inputs.

Sixty years of supplying growers across the southern districts sits behind the proportions, and the formulation is reviewed as better varieties become available.

Establishment is the critical phase. The paddock should be shut up and left ungrazed until plants are well anchored and cannot be pulled from the soil, which may be eight to ten months after sowing.

details.description:
The Western Annual Mix is available exclusively through Landmark branches and agents, and it is an Irwin Hunter formulation drawing on sixty years of watching annual ryegrasses perform across Western Australia.

The mix is continually reviewed and updated with the most proven varieties for local conditions rather than being left to stand. It currently combines Abundant Tetraploid and Dargo Diploid, two of the best known performers in the state, both adaptable and highly productive across a wide range of soil types from Geraldton in the north through to the southern country around Esperance.

Blending a tetraploid with a diploid is a deliberate choice rather than a convenience. Tetraploid seed is larger and the plant more palatable, driving intake; diploid seed is smaller, so the same weight of seed puts more plants in the ground, and the diploid component adds tiller density and persistence. Sown together they produce more, and eat better, than either would alone.

It suits growers wanting a dependable, high production annual pasture for grazing, silage or hay, without having to work out the blend themselves.
